docs.title: KD Equation discovery from data
docs.text:
KD is a symbolic regression library for discovering equations from field data, ODE trajectories and feature tables. It provides data preparation, search and result analysis through a Python API and a local browser interface.

Get started Tutorials Documentation

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
pip install sail-kd

import kd
# Bundled Burgers field: 256 × 201 (x, t)
data = kd.load_burgers()

model = kd.Model(
    algorithm="sga", generations=5, seed=0
).fit(data)
Recorded result · 5 generations · AIC -28.78 \(u_t =\)\(-u\,u_x\)\(+0.1002\,u_{xx}\) Full guide

docs.title: About and citation
docs.text:
open source · apache 2.0 About KD

KD is a platform for discovering governing equations from data, developed at the Scientific Artificial Intelligence Lab. It gives equation-discovery algorithms one interface and one set of shared services, and the whole platform is open source.

github Source code The platform, its algorithm plugins, the bundled datasets and the runnable examples. github Issues Report a problem, ask a question, or propose an algorithm to add. apache 2.0 License KD is released under the Apache License, Version 2.0.

docs.title: Credit
docs.text: The algorithms KD runs are implementations of published methods, and the work behind each one belongs to its authors. Every algorithm page names the paper it comes from and links the authors' own code under References. The two sets of real measurements that ship with KD are cited on Bundled datasets.

docs.title: Citation
docs.text: For research using KD, cite the original works for the algorithms and datasets you use. The algorithm pages provide the method papers; dataset documentation provides sources and attribution. The repository's CITATION.cff contains the project citation metadata.

docs.title: Algorithms
docs.text: KD puts seven equation-discovery algorithms behind one intermediate representation and one API: switching algorithms means changing kd.Model(algorithm=...), with the same dataset and the same way of reading the result. The derivatives are computed by the platform to each algorithm's declared requirement, so their source can differ (see derivative sources). Each algorithm constructs its own final score, so those numbers do not line up across algorithms; refit the same terms in one context with evaluate_terms first, as described in score conventions and comparability.

docs.text:

docs.title: Search space
docs.text:
DISCOVER samples expression trees from operator and variable tokens, without a fixed candidate-term library. In the PDE vocabulary, products, quotients and trigonometric expressions can use the dataset's fields and coordinates, with spatial derivatives represented by diff_<axis>(...) and diff2_<axis>(...) for each spatial axis (diff_x(u) and diff2_x(u) for a field u on an axis x). Repeated multiplication forms powers. Priors restrict nesting of derivatives and trigonometric functions. Coordinate tokens permit coordinate-dependent fits.

The facade builds the grid vocabulary from the dataset: every field is a leaf, sorted by name (the target is the left-hand side, not a token); the spatial axes, in the dataset's order, and t are coordinate leaves; and each spatial axis adds diff_<axis> and diff2_<axis>. Spatial axes other than x and y are refused. A library set in the Python configuration is used as given and refuses a field or axis it does not name. The vocabulary contains no mixed derivative or third-order derivative token. Outside sketch compilation, max_diff_order leaves sampling unchanged: expressions above its cumulative derivative-order cap are rejected after sampling and still use a batch slot. Sketch compilation can also narrow derivative tokens using the sketch bounds. Neither path adds absent tokens or overrides other structural priors. The vocabulary a run searched is sealed in its result config as searched_vocabulary (operators, state and coordinate variables, and the engine's token names and arities; on a sketch run, the library narrowed to the sketch), so it is read there rather than reconstructed from the requested configuration. The facade controls iteration count with generations; n_iterations does not set its loop length. Without pinn, the PDE path evaluates derivatives from the observed grid by finite differences and requires no pretrained weights or optional backend. With pinn set, the same vocabulary is searched in PINN mode, where a neural network is trained on the data and derivatives are taken from the network by automatic differentiation.

MODE1 and MODE2 accept target_lhs_order=1 (the default) or 2, matching the dataset's declared target. Order 2 fits the second time derivative directly; it does not add time-derivative tokens to the default RHS vocabulary. PINN search targets and physics residuals use the same order. Tabular mode refuses a nondefault PDE target order. Changing the target order starts a new lineage.

docs.title: Tabular regression
docs.text: Tabular mode is selected by the input data, without a mode parameter. Its vocabulary is derived from the feature columns plus add, sub, mul, div, sin, cos, exp, log and a fitted const terminal. No derivative tokens or configured term library are used. Each distinct candidate's constants are fitted before scoring. The recurrent controller and training rule remain the same, while complexity counts tokens instead of additive terms.

docs.title: Method
docs.text:
An LSTM samples token sequences in pre-order, conditioned on the parent and left sibling of each slot. Structural priors mask illegal choices: expression length and token-repetition bounds, addition or subtraction below a derivative, derivative arguments other than fields or permitted derivative expressions, and unary operators directly below their inverse. The standard priors also prevent nested derivatives and trigonometric nesting. Sequences that fail length or legality checks, including cumulative derivative order above max_diff_order, are dropped after sampling, and surviving expressions are deduplicated before scoring.

In PDE mode the platform splits top-level additions into terms, fits their coefficients by dense least squares against the time derivative, and computes NMSE. Subtraction is carried by signed terms. In tabular mode, all-constant candidates are rejected; unique traversals fit constants with a scale-free BFGS objective before serialization as numeric literals. The platform then scores the whole expression as one regression term with a fitted outer scale.

Risk-seeking policy gradient retains the top epsilon fraction of valid rewards, subtracts a scalar baseline, and takes an Adam step on the policy loss plus an entropy bonus. Invalid fits receive zero reward and are excluded from training. The champion changes only on strict improvement, so ties retain the incumbent. The seed controls both initial network weights and token sampling. One controller iteration is one KD iteration, controlled by generations.

Pin reservation under a sketch excludes shared jet monomials, but does not cover every rational respelling or several separately admitted terms whose sum reconstructs a pinned column. The compile notes describe these limits.

docs.title: PINN mode
docs.text:
Setting pinn on grid data selects PINN mode. On a fresh call, a fully connected network is first pretrained on the observations: every grid point, or the share given by obs_ratio. A resumed call loads the stored network without pretraining. Candidates are then scored on collocation points sampled inside the data domain, with the time derivative on the left-hand side and every spatial derivative taken from the network by automatic differentiation.

After n_iterations generations, and then after every cycle_n_iterations generations, the network is retrained on the data loss plus coef_pde times the residual of the best equation found so far, and the search continues on the derivatives of the retrained network. The champion is re-scored on each new network before the search resumes. On a fresh call, generations is the total number of search generations, so a retraining phase runs only when n_iterations is smaller than generations. On resume, the phase boundaries use the generation count over all segments of the run; the resumed call's generations add to that count. A phase on a call's last generation is not run in that call. If the earlier segment ended on such a boundary, the resumed call runs that phase first, before its first generation. When stability_selection is positive, the final equation is chosen among the top candidates of the last cycle by refitting each on bootstrap resamples.

The time of the pretraining and of each retraining phase grows with the number of epochs times the number of training points. The library defaults of pretrain_epoch, pinn_epoch and n_collocation are the research budget of the reference configuration.

docs.title: Result interpretation
docs.text:
The reward combines fit and complexity as (1 - reward_alpha * complexity) / (1 + sqrt(nmse)), clipped to [0, 1]. Complexity is the term count for PDEs and token count for tables. NMSE alone does not rank expressions. A surviving coordinate term indicates dependence on that coordinate and should be interpreted according to the physical model being sought.

For PDEs, model.best_expr_ is the sampled structure and model.result_.equation carries the coefficients from the same least-squares fit used in scoring. In ordinary MODE1, the recorder's best_reward does not decrease within a call. In PINN mode each phase re-prices the champion on the new network, so the value can fall, to zero if the champion is invalid.

n_eval_valid distinguishes invalid sampling from valid candidates with poor fits. An improving champion at the final iteration suggests additional search may still change the result; a flat curve alone does not identify the cause.

In PINN mode the final equation is fitted on the collocation points, so the target and the residuals of the result have one entry per collocation point, and the result config records provider_kind as autograd. On a fresh call, the recorder carries the pretraining outcome in the pinn_pretrain_* series; a resumed segment's recorder has no such series. Each segment records one entry per retraining phase it executes in pinn_cycle_idx, pinn_phase_ran, pinn_best_reward, pinn_data_loss, pinn_physics_loss, pinn_total_loss, pinn_epochs_run and pinn_train_seconds. A phase with no valid best equation is recorded with pinn_phase_ran equal to 0 and leaves the network unchanged.

Tabular results carry a REGRESSION equation with the target column on the left. The expression retains its fitted numeric literals and one outer least-squares scale. model.result_.pareto_front() exposes nondominated expressions with their token counts, loss and outer scale; the corresponding series are pareto_expressions, pareto_complexity, pareto_loss and pareto_scale. The inner constants and outer scale are distinct fitted values.

docs.title: Python setup
docs.text: A kd.TabularDataset selects tabular mode in Model.fit(). A typed DiscoverConfig can supply a different library, which is Python-only and unavailable through JSON params. pinn takes a PINNConfig, exported from kd.search, or a JSON object of its fields, in which every omitted key keeps its default. DiscoverConfig.burgers_preset(pinn=PINNConfig(...)) combines a reference preset with PINN mode through config=. An EarlyStoppingCallback and a kd.TabularDataset are refused together with pinn. A sketch is accepted with pinn: its pins are deducted from every rebuilt collocation target and enter the PINN residual.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
Du et al. (2024). "DISCOVER: Deep identification of symbolically concise open-form partial differential equations via enhanced reinforcement learning". Phys. Rev. Research 6, 013182. Paper · arXiv:2210.02181

Code: menggedu/DISCOVER

Implementation notes. KD implements the reinforcement-learning search, structural priors, PINN mode and its optional stability selection. The paper's genetic operators and dynamic subtree bank are not implemented. Risk-seeking policy gradient is the training strategy; PQT has zero weight in the reference's shipped configuration, and PPO is not implemented. Grid fits default to quantile 0.10 with batch size 16; tabular fits default to 0.05 with batch size 500. DSO-PyTorch used 0.05 and the paper used 0.02. Unary diff_x(u) replaces the paper's binary diff(u, x) for one-dimensional spatial differentiation.

Dense least squares and the stability-selection statistic std / mean follow the reference code; the paper prints the reciprocal statistic. The optional coefficient-magnitude rejection is disabled unless configured. A follow-up method trains a neural surrogate and differentiates it by autograd; KD runs it as PINN mode. The retraining phases are placed inside the generations loop by n_iterations and cycle_n_iterations, and the reference's cycle count n_cycles is read only by the standalone cycle runner.

docs.title: Worked example
docs.text:
The run below uses the Chafee-Infante dataset that ships with KD: a 301 × 200 grid over x in [0, 3] and t in [0.1, 0.5], carrying a single hump held at zero at both ends of the interval. Above u = 1 the cubic term is larger than the linear one, so the hump climbs from 1.94 at the first time step to 4.67 at the last while diffusion keeps its profile smooth.

The observed field over its physical spatial and time coordinates.

The equation returned by the run:

Equation Discovered \(u_{t} = 0.9808 t^{3} u + 0.9808 u^{3} - 0.9946 u + 0.9754 u_{xx}\) Reference \(u_t = u_{xx} -u +u^3\)

The returned expression contains the reference diffusion and reaction terms, plus a time-dependent cubic contribution. The displayed coefficients are fitted on this run. The search receives operator tokens (add, mul, div, diff_x, diff2_x, diff3_x, n2, n3) and composes the candidate expressions.

The fitted derivative target, its equation prediction, and predicted minus measured values. The first two panels share a color scale; the residual has its own scale, with any clipping disclosed on the figure.

docs.title: Example diagnostics
docs.text:
This run has reward 0.955317 and NMSE 0.0002362.

The reward divides a term-count penalty by one plus the square root of NMSE. Every derivative in this run is a finite difference of the observations.

The search is recorded as well. kd.VizEngine renders the per-iteration record; alongside the universal convergence curve, DISCOVER contributes four diagnostic panels of its own, three of which this run drew (the full list is under Visualization):

The best native score is shown above the algorithm's population diagnostic, when one is recorded. Each panel retains its own score scale. The algorithm's diagnostic panels, using the same data and plot functions as the full report. 
viz = kd.VizEngine(output_dir="out/chafee-infante")
viz.render_all(model.result_, algorithm=model.algorithm_, dataset=dataset)

docs.title: Tabular example
docs.text:
config = DiscoverConfig(
    seed=0, batch_size=1000, max_length=15, reward_alpha=0.005
)
model = kd.Model(algorithm="discover", generations=200, config=config)
model.fit(kd.load_tlc_cc())

The table layout is described under data requirements.

The run below uses that table. Its 74 rows come from an automated column-chromatography platform: the features are the thin-layer retardation factor R_F and the petroleum-ether fraction r of the eluent, and the target is the retention volume V_S in millilitres. A formula relating the three has been published for this table (Xu et al., 2025). The settings are seed 0, 200 iterations, 1000 draws per iteration, expressions of at most 15 tokens, and reward_alpha 0.005.

Equation Discovered \(V_S = \dfrac{r}{0.1507\,R_F + 0.0111}\) Reference \(V_S = \dfrac{r}{0.147\,R_F + 0.0114}\)

Both rows are written as r / (a R_F + b). Scoring is scale-free, so the search returns a bare expression with the outer coefficient fitted beside it, and this answer arrived as 6.634 times r / (R_F + 0.0737); dividing through puts it in the published form. The two coefficients land 2.5% and 2.6% from the published pair, from one run at a fixed seed, with the search given four arithmetic operators and two column names rather than any candidate terms.

That expression is five tokens long, and it is an entry on the run's Pareto front rather than the answer the run selected. Three of the 74 rows were measured at r = 0, where the formula returns zero against measured volumes of 4.41, 5.17 and 5.86 mL. The selected expression returns nonzero volumes at r = 0 and fits the table more closely: nine tokens, at an nmse of 0.1021 against the five-token law's 0.1235.

The final Pareto table lists complexity, loss, outer scale and mathematical expression for each candidate. Compare the five-token law with the selected nine-token expression using the values in the table. Predicted values against the measured target, with the diagonal denoting exact agreement and R² computed over the full fit. The best native score is shown above the algorithm's population diagnostic, when one is recorded. Each panel retains its own score scale.

docs.title: Search space
docs.text:
DLGA-PDE searches sums of products drawn from a candidate library, fitting constant coefficients. Reachable expressions are polynomials in the supplied field and derivative tokens. Use the dataset's own field and axis names: u_x_t is a mixed partial, and diff_t(u_x) is its open-form spelling. An atomic name segment is limited to third order; higher compound derivatives can be written as u_xx_xx.

The library determines which axes can enter a result. A library token that names an unknown field or axis, or a dataset field other than the left-hand-side one, refuses the whole fit before training. So does, when no sketch is set, a token that spells a time derivative of the left-hand-side field that the run fits: the order target_lhs_order names (u_t, diff_t(u), diff1_t(u) for order 1; u_tt, diff2_t(u) for order 2), or both orders while lhs_auto_select is on. Such a token would fit its own branch exactly. The time derivative of an order the run does not fit is an ordinary library token. An atomic segment above third order, such as u_xxxx, is not refused: the fit runs and every candidate containing that token is invalid, so use the u_xx_xx spelling. The surrogate models only the left-hand-side field; other fields and their derivatives cannot enter its library. The constant-coefficient stage is implemented; the adaptive variable-coefficient modes are rejected at construction.

Surrogate fitting precedes genetic search and can dominate cost. Both the number of observations and the derivative library affect resource use; the epoch budget alone does not bound memory. A shorter fit changes derivative accuracy and, under lhs_auto_select, can change the selected left-hand-side order. No pretrained weights or optional backend are needed.

docs.title: Method
docs.text:
A neural network first fits the observations over their coordinates. The architecture has five hidden layers of 50 units, sin activation and Adam optimization. Field reads and derivatives both come from this network, with derivatives obtained by autograd.

A genome contains up to max_modules modules of up to max_module_length tokens. Each module is a product and the genome is their sum. Coefficients are found from the augmented system's null space or by ordinary least squares, according to solver. Fitness is nmse + epsilon * length, with length counted in tokens. Each candidate is fitted against the time derivative of the order target_lhs_order names, which has to equal the dataset's own left-hand-side order. With lhs_auto_select enabled, each candidate is fitted against both the first and second time derivative and the branch with the lower NMSE is used, so the returned law can carry the order the dataset does not declare. A sketch overrides lhs_auto_select: candidates fit only its left-hand-side order. If the admitted sketch holes allow no products, compilation limits each searched module to one token.

Each generation scores the population, retains the better half, refills it with random genomes, exchanges a module between adjacent pairs, then mutates by adding or deleting a module and shifting a token to an adjacent library entry. Library order therefore affects mutation. One generation is one KD iteration, controlled by generations.

docs.title: Result interpretation
docs.text:
model.best_score_ combines the fit error with the per-token length penalty, so NMSE alone does not rank term sets. NMSE is measured against the network's field and derivatives, which are the quantities used during search. model.result_.equation carries the fitted terms, coefficients and selected left-hand side. The returned coefficients come from KD's refit over the selected structure on that surrogate domain.

The recorder distinguishes surrogate training from genetic search. Read the training and validation losses alongside the per-generation fitness, diversity and complexity series. Training loss series are absent when the network is injected or restored from a checkpoint, since that call trains no network. A small NMSE is evidence of a fit on that domain, and does not by itself establish recovery of the generating equation. If changing the population budget improves the result, the search budget was relevant. On a fresh call without an injected network, seed also controls network training. With an injected or checkpoint-restored network, changing the seed varies only the genetic search. Repeated poor fits also warrant checking the library and surrogate accuracy.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
Xu et al. (2020). "DLGA-PDE: Discovery of PDEs with incomplete candidate library via combination of deep learning and genetic algorithm". J. Comput. Phys. 418, 109584. Paper · arXiv:2001.07305

Code: woshixuhao/DLGA_tutorial (the author's tutorial notebook, on the KdV case), woshixuhao/PIC_code (the author's own code for a later paper, running the same neural-network-plus-genetic-algorithm search)

Implementation notes. The paper treats the order of the time derivative as part of what is discovered: the left-hand side is a gene of the genome, changed by mutation, and genomes with different left-hand sides compete on fitness. By default KD takes the order from the dataset and fits only that left-hand side. An earlier implementation fits u_t and u_tt for every candidate and keeps the better branch, which is lhs_auto_select=true here; under that option KD compares the branches by NMSE. The paper's Eq. (6) and that implementation compare raw MSE, which also varies with the target branch's variance. The length penalty is configurable; the author's tutorial fixes it for its demonstration. The genetic mechanism is checked against that implementation, with corrected crossover indexing and selection of candidates with duplicate fitness values. KD mutates a nonzero gene by one library index in either direction; index zero can redraw any library index. The earlier implementation redraws the selected gene uniformly from 0 to 3. The adaptive variable-coefficient extension is not part of this implementation.

docs.title: Worked example
docs.text:
The run below uses the Burgers dataset that ships with KD: a 256 × 201 grid over x in [-8, 8) and t in [0, 10], whose initial profile steepens into a front at the origin and then spreads out as the diffusive term takes over.

The observed field over its physical spatial and time coordinates.

The equation returned by the run:

Equation Discovered \(u_{t} = - 0.9993 u u_{x} + 0.0999 u_{xx}\) Reference \(u_t = -u\,u_x +0.1\,u_{xx}\)

Both terms and both coefficients match. The terms were assembled from the default candidate library (u, u_x, u_xx, u_xxx), and every candidate was fitted against u_t alone under the default target_lhs_order=1 and lhs_auto_select=False. Setting lhs_auto_select=True enables the paper's two-branch selection, fitting each candidate against both u_t and u_tt and keeping the branch with the lower NMSE.

A pretrained transformer proposes equations and is fine-tuned on candidates ranked by their fit to data.

dataset = kd.generate_burgers_data(nx=256, nt=101, nu=0.1, seed=42)
model = kd.Model(algorithm="eqgpt", generations=15, config=EqGPTConfig.burgers_preset())

docs.title: Search space
docs.text:
EqGPT samples equations from a fixed vocabulary of terms, then fits their coefficients against data. The single-case evolution path uses one field u, time axis t and one to three spatial axes named x, y or z. In evolution mode the prefix S ut + fixes the left-hand side, and right-hand-side terms combine atoms by multiplication, division and addition. The vocabulary comes with KD; no candidate-term library is supplied by the caller.

Sampling masks tokens containing t, tokens referring to absent axes, derivatives beyond the active provider's order, tokens without an IR mapping, masked_tokens and, under a sketch, tokens the sketch excludes. On a time axis and one spatial axis x, the evolution finite-difference path admits these 21 atoms: u, ux, uxx, uxxx, ux^2, u^2, u^3, x, x^2, x^4, sin(u), sinx, exp(x), (uux)x, (uux)xx, (u^3)xx, (u^4)xx, (1/u)xx, (u^-2*ux)x, (u(u^2)xx)xx and (uxx+ux/x)^2. Higher atomic x-derivatives exceed that provider's cap; mixed space-time terms, explicit time dependence, sqrt and sinh are not in this search space.

Sentence gates give zero reward to the term combinations {u, sin(u)}, {u, sinh(u)}, {sin(u), sinh(u)}, {u, u^2, u^3} and {x, sinx}. Another gate requires every declared axis to occur unless the sentence contains Laplace. It tests substrings of the joined sentence, so exp(-y) also counts as containing x; under a sketch, axes carried by pinned terms count as present. The pinned ut covers time, so an evolution candidate must also represent its spatial axes. These gates act before fitting.

For a steady problem on scattered (x, y) coordinates, configure steady, steady_activation and start_words=["S"] together. This mode trains its own surrogate before search. sparsity_alpha is required because the appropriate penalty depends on the problem; the packaged presets supply explicit values. Boundary deletion (steady_boundary_delete_num) counts cells on a grid that by default consists of the distinct coordinate values in the data, so a grid row or column without data points is missing from it. steady_boundary_grid gives the grid explicitly, and the presets that enable boundary deletion set it; the dataset name does not affect the grid.

docs.title: Method
docs.text:
The proposer is a decoder-only transformer with six layers, eight heads, model dimension 768 and a context of 50, over 56 vocabulary tokens plus a pad slot. It is pretrained on equations collected from mathematical handbooks. Sampling alternates between a term token and E, +, * or /. With probability exploration_rate, a token is drawn uniformly from the legal set; otherwise the transformer evaluates the current prefix.

Each accepted sentence converts to KD IR terms, and the platform executes one column per term. Least squares fits the relation and the reward combines centered R² with a penalty on the column count. Each epoch merges candidates into a reward-deduplicated elite pool of at most top_k entries. The size of its first fill is retained for the rest of the run. It then fine-tunes on that pool with Adam at finetune_lr for finetune_steps steps. One epoch is one KD iteration, controlled by generations.

docs.title: Result interpretation
docs.text:
The reward is R² * (1 - sparsity_alpha * log10(k)), where k counts distinct columns including the pinned left-hand-side column. R² measures the derivative fit in evolution mode. The penalty lowers the attainable reward as columns are added; it is not an NMSE alone. A zero reward can result from a sentence gate, while a negative reward is a fitted relation worse than predicting the mean. Candidates that fail execution or matrix construction can be discarded before reaching the pool; no candidate is an invalid result.

model.best_expr_ lists structural terms without fitted coefficients. model.result_.equation carries the native fitted coefficients aligned with those terms. Evolution-mode final coefficients and NMSE are evaluated on the full coefficient domain against the un-negated time derivative; that domain can differ from the sampled reward domain. IR uses names such as u_x, u_xx, n2(u), diff_x(mul(u, u_x)) and diff2_x(mul(u, u_x)), rather than the vocabulary's ux, uxx, u^2, (uux)x and (uux)xx.

The per-epoch record includes pool reward statistics and fine-tuning loss. A low reward warrants checking whether the required atoms and combinations are expressible before increasing the sample budget. Because the prior was trained on named textbook equations, a familiar law can be proposed from that prior as well as selected by its fit to data.

docs.title: Pretrained model
docs.text: The checkpoint is downloaded from the KD Hub mirror on first use and cached. An uncached run needs network access. KD_EQGPT_ASSET_DIR can point to a local directory containing gpt_model/PDEGPT_wave_breaking.pt; the Python API also accepts EqGPTConfig(weights_path=...) or asset_dir. The mirror is timeoutHao/KD-data, with a pinned revision and SHA-256 verification. Multi-case wave mode also needs WaveBreaking.pkl and per-case surrogates. Surrogates resolve through v1_asset_dir, then KD_V1_WAVE_ASSETS, then the Hub mirror. The pickle is not downloaded: in a source checkout its default is data/hf-knowledgediscover/WaveBreaking.pkl relative to the repository. Wheel users should supply wave_pkl_path. Both wave_pkl_path and v1_asset_dir are Python-only configuration fields. The dataset passed to fit in this mode must equal the data of the primary case (primary_case): axis order, field names and every coordinate and field value are compared, and only the name may differ.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
Xu et al. (2025). "Generative discovery of partial differential equations by learning from math handbooks". Nat. Commun. 16, 10255. Paper

Code: woshixuhao/EqGPT

Implementation notes. KD drives the published checkpoint through its own sampler and reward. The unused decoder-encoder attention submodule is omitted; forward equivalence was checked on checkpoint logits, and the vocabulary is copied byte for byte. Sampling follows the same legal mechanism without reproducing the reference's random stream. Evolution mode uses platform finite differences where the reference used autograd surrogates, which changes the available high-order atoms. Malformed and length-truncated sentences are discarded; degenerate reward matrices receive zero, and least squares uses rcond=None. The reference's fixed elite-pool size is configurable as top_k.

The plugin runs the single-case pipeline and the multi-case wave-breaking pipeline, where one structure is fitted across 12 experiments. Multi-case reward averages the cases scored successfully.

The terms come from the distribution the model learned over token sequences, and the coefficients from the least-squares fit of the selected equation.

docs.text:
A large language model proposes and revises candidate equations round by round, filtered by a sparse reward.

algorithmllm4edscoreLLM4ED sparse reward maxcostmediumderivativesfinite_diffequation formEVOLUTION REGRESSIONdata layoutgrid tabular

docs.title: Usage

from kd import Llm4edConfig

dataset = kd.load_llm4ed_heat()
model = kd.Model(
    algorithm="llm4ed",
    generations=12,
    config=Llm4edConfig(base_url="https://api.openai.com/v1"),

model.fit(dataset)

docs.text: Parameter Default Resume Description temperature 0.8 resume-safe LLM sampling temperature. max_tokens 1024 resume-safe Maximum decoded tokens per request. stop_threshold 0.995 resume-safe Reward threshold for completion. fit_stop_threshold None resume-safe Optional completion threshold for the best sparse-reward candidate's unrounded 1/(1+NRMSE). None disables fit stopping. reward_limit 0.5 resume-safe Minimum admitted sparse reward. pool_size 5 resume-safe Elite-pool capacity. All fields of Llm4edConfig Field Type Default temperature float 0.8 max_tokens int 1024 stop_threshold float 0.995 reward_limit float 0.5 pool_size int 5 init_num int 20 samples_per_epoch int 8 max_llm_calls_per_propose int 50 max_llm_calls_per_run int 200 seed int 0 model str gpt-4o-mini base_url str \| None None tape_record_path str \| None None extra_body dict[str, Any] \| None None functions tuple[str, ...] () edge_trim int 0 l0_penalty float 1e-05 l0_relative bool False max_derivative_order int 3 fit_stop_threshold float \| None None

docs.title: Search space
docs.text:
LLM4ED asks a language model for coefficient-free equations over a fixed symbol library and fits their coefficients by sparse regression. Its PDE mode operates on one scalar field with one time axis and spatial axes x, y or both. The symbols are the field u and, for each spatial axis present, its coordinate and the derivatives along it: x, u_x, u_xx, u_xxx and y, u_y, u_yy, u_yyy. The prompts specify +, -, *, /, squares and cubes; the parser also accepts integer powers through five. Explicit spatial dependence is expressible. Extra fields, other-axis derivatives, mixed space-time derivatives, higher spatial derivatives, trigonometric functions, exponentials, square roots and standalone constants are outside this route's symbol library. Extra fields and spatial axes other than x and y are refused before proposal generation.

Operand construction needs at least four spatial and three time points. Spacing is taken from x[2] - x[1] and t[1] - t[0], so use uniform axes. The method itself does not smooth or train a surrogate; the platform's savgol_window applies before differentiation. Higher derivatives therefore depend on measurement noise and resolution.

docs.title: Tabular regression
docs.text:
Tabular data selects the tabular mode, without a mode parameter. The symbols are the table's feature columns, and the target column is the left-hand side; no derivatives are computed. The prompts offer +, -, *, /, squares and cubes and the functions named in functions, any of sin, cos, exp, log and sqrt; the default is none, and the PDE mode refuses a non-empty value. The parser accepts integer powers through five, and with sqrt a half-integer power of magnitude at most five, such as x**(3/2), reads as an integer power of sqrt(x). A feature or target named c1, c2, ... is refused, and so is a name the SymPy parser does not read back as one plain symbol.

The prompts ask for each constant inside a term as a placeholder c1, c2, ..., pi and e included; integers may be written directly, and the prompts ask for no decimal numbers. The parser keeps a placeholder wherever it appears and reads a decimal like any other number. A nonzero numeric term, or a term of placeholders alone (c1, 2*c1, sin(c1)), is an intercept column on one whose value is the fitted coefficient; several such terms merge into one intercept. A term whose value is a non-numeric constant, such as pi or log(2), makes the candidate invalid, and so does a constant term of zero, which is what x - x expands to. SymPy expands each proposal before it is split into terms, so exp(x + 1) becomes E*exp(x) and log(2*x) becomes log(2) + log(x); both are invalid for their non-numeric constant.

docs.title: Method
docs.text:
The language model receives the symbol library and scored proposal history, not the observed arrays. The first round requests a numbered batch of coefficient-free equations. Later rounds alternate an optimization prompt, which lists earlier equations in ascending score order and asks for improved ones, with an evolution prompt that requests selection, crossover and mutation of term sets.

Each proposal is parsed with SymPy, expanded into additive terms, and executed as design-matrix columns over second-order finite-difference operands. Division allows reciprocals, but a zero denominator that makes a column non-finite rejects that candidate. STRidge sweeps a tolerance ladder to fit coefficients; fitted coefficient magnitudes outside [1e-4, 1e4] also reject a candidate.

In the tabular mode the operands are the table's columns. Division and the functions use their ordinary definitions, so a zero denominator, log or sqrt of a negative value, or an exp that overflows gives a non-finite column and rejects the candidate. Before the columns are built, the placeholders of one equation are fitted together; a name used in several terms is one constant. For given values every term is executed into a column, the outer coefficients are the least-squares solution over all terms, and the objective is the residual sum of squares divided by y @ y for the target column y (the plain sum when y is all zero). BFGS with gradient tolerance 1e-10 runs once from each of the fixed starts 1.0, -1.0 and 0.1, with every placeholder at the start value, and the start with the smallest objective wins. The terms then carry the fitted values as numeric literals, and STRidge fits the outer coefficients as in the PDE mode; terms it sets to zero do not cause a refit of the constants. The fit is local: a constant that BFGS does not reach from any of the three starts is not found, and whether it is found can depend on the range of the data. A placeholder that only scales its term, as in c1*x, is not identified apart from the outer coefficient; its fitted value, and with it the size of the outer coefficient, depends on the start that wins, and an outer coefficient outside [1e-4, 1e4] rejects the candidate.

Within one tabular equation, two columns that are equal or opposite elementwise, within 1e-9 of the larger column's maximum magnitude, are one term; the PDE mode keeps the reference's rule based on absolute sums. After the fit, two terms with nonzero coefficients that differ only in numeric constants, such as sin(0.5*x1) and sin(1.5*x1), make the candidate invalid (counted as inexpressible): the REGRESSION equation identifies a term by its structure without literals and cannot hold both.

A round resamples until enough distinct-scoring survivors arrive or its call budget is exhausted. Scores at or below reward_limit and scores already kept in the round are discarded. The best samples_per_epoch survivors are offered to an elite pool of pool_size; after filling, it admits only a strict improvement over its minimum with an unseen score. The next prompt receives that batch and the pool as it stood before the update. One round is one KD iteration, controlled by generations. Per-round and per-run call limits bound endpoint requests. Once the run limit is exhausted, subsequent rounds can return no proposals; a stop threshold above the attainable reward cannot end the search early.

docs.title: Result interpretation
docs.text:
The sparse reward is (1 - 0.01 * k) / (1 + RMSE / std(target)), where k counts fitted nonzero coefficients and is capped at five. It is rounded to four decimals before ranking and duplicate filtering. A one-term perfect fit reaches 0.99, three terms reach 0.97 and four terms reach 0.96. The same reward therefore implies different errors for different support sizes. Before rounding, the inverse is nmse = ((1 - 0.01 * k) / reward - 1)**2. In the tabular mode a nonzero intercept counts toward k like any other column, and fitted placeholder constants do not count; the reference has neither, so these counts have no reference value.

The returned law contains only surviving structural terms and their native sparse-fit coefficients. Terms whose coefficients were zeroed are removed from both lists. model.result_.equation carries the aligned values, and NMSE and MSE use the finite-difference domain that supplied the candidate columns, or the table's rows in the tabular mode. A tabular law is a REGRESSION equation with the target column on the left; its terms carry the fitted constants as numeric literals, while the proposal history shown to the language model keeps the placeholders. A tabular checkpoint records the mode and functions; a restore into the other mode or under different functions is refused.

The per-round recorder includes pool_best, pool_median, pool_worst, n_valid, n_invalid and n_llm_calls. The admitted count n_valid is measured after truncation and saturates at samples_per_epoch. n_invalid counts dropped scoring events, broken down into eight series: n_invalid_undefined_operands, n_invalid_undefined_operators, n_invalid_inexpressible, n_invalid_parse, n_invalid_non_finite, n_invalid_lstsq, n_invalid_abnormal_coef and n_invalid_other. They sum to the total in each round; unused causes record zero, and other collects labels outside those named categories. Pool progress and admissions help distinguish proposal failures from valid but poorly fitting equations.

docs.title: Endpoint configuration
docs.text: Set an OpenAI-compatible base_url and OPENAI_API_KEY for the default client; the OpenAI SDK is installed with KD. This is the algorithm that calls an external language-model service during search. Alternatively, pass a provider= implementing kd.llm.LLMProvider: a prompt goes in and text comes out. A custom client can set timeouts and headers, use BudgetedProvider for metering, or use TapeRecordingProvider to save a JSONL tape for offline replay. The authors' mirrored datasets download on first load.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
Du et al. (2024). "Large language models for automatic equation discovery of nonlinear dynamics". Phys. Fluids 36, 097121. Paper · arXiv:2405.07761

Code: menggedu/EDL

Implementation notes. KD ports the reference's finite-difference templates, STRidge tolerance sweep, coefficient gate, reward formula and rounding. The NumPy STRidge port matches its reference on identical design matrices. Prompt term permutation uses a plugin-owned seeded generator, including on resume. Columns use KD's executor instead of NumPy lambdify, so floating-point differences can affect candidates near the coefficient gate. Single-character candidates are scored rather than skipped. In the PDE mode, constructs outside the prompt vocabulary, such as trigonometric functions and non-integer exponents, are rejected explicitly. The call budgets are KD additions, and so is the tabular mode with its prompt templates, placeholder fit, intercept and elementwise duplicate rule; the reference's three PDE templates are unchanged. The paper used GPT-3.5-turbo; the KD client accepts OpenAI-compatible endpoints. The method's contribution is the prompting loop that generates equations and evaluates them by sparse regression.

docs.title: Worked example
docs.text:
The run below uses the heat-equation dataset from the LLM4ED authors, mirrored on Hugging Face Hub: a 200 × 201 grid over x in [0, 9.95] with periodic boundaries and t in [0, 10]. The initial profile is a localized oscillation centred near x = 5, a positive lobe at x = 4.55 against a negative one at x = 5.45 with weaker lobes to either side, and diffusion spreads and flattens it: the amplitude falls from 0.89 at t = 0 to 0.049 at t = 10, half of it gone by t = 1.45.

The observed field over its physical spatial and time coordinates.

The recorded requests and responses were replayed offline for twelve rounds. The original endpoint served nvidia/llama-3.3-nemotron-super-49b-v1.5, with a limit of six calls per round and seed 42. The equation returned by the run:

Equation Discovered \(u_{t} = 0.05014 u_{xx}\) Reference \(u_t = 0.05\,u_{xx}\)

The term and the coefficient match. The model wrote a two-term right-hand side, u_xx + u u_x; the sparse regression fitted the second coefficient to zero, so one term survives and the reward counts one term.

docs.title: PySINDy
docs.text:
Sparse regression over a supplied candidate library, solved in one pass.

algorithmpysindyscoreNMSE mincostlightderivativesfinite_diffequation formEVOLUTION REGRESSIONdata layoutgrid tabular

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
import kd

dataset = kd.load_burgers()
config = kd.PySINDyConfig(
    terms=("u", "u_x", "u_xx", "mul(u,u_x)"), threshold=0.05, seed=0,
)
model = kd.Model(algorithm="pysindy", config=config)
model.fit(dataset)
print(model.result_.equation)

docs.title: Main parameters
docs.text: Parameter Default Resume Description threshold 0.1 init-only STLSQ sparsity threshold. max_iter 20 init-only Maximum STLSQ iterations. normalize_columns False init-only Normalize library columns before STLSQ. relative_threshold False init-only Read threshold as a fraction of the target L2 norm (requires normalize_columns). degree 2 init-only Maximum total polynomial degree for tabular data. All fields of PySINDyConfig Field Type Default terms tuple[str, ...] ('u', 'u_x', 'u_xx', 'mul(u, u_x)') threshold float 0.1 max_iter int 20 normalize_columns bool False relative_threshold bool False unbias bool True alpha float 0.05 seed int 0 extra_optimizer_kwargs dict[str, Any] \| None None degree int 2 target_lhs_order int 1

docs.title: Search space
docs.text:
The KD wrapper uses PySINDy's sparse optimizer over a supplied term library. terms contains KD function-call strings using the dataset's field and axis names. Supply terms for grids other than one-field u with spatial axes x, y or both; on those the default terms are u and, for each spatial axis a, u_a, u_aa and mul(u, u_a). mul and add take two arguments; nest multiplication for a cube. Terms can contain coordinates, products such as mul(u, u_x), and operators such as sin, exp or binary div. A compound derivative uses u_x_t or diff_t(u_x) rather than u_xt. Supplied terms are used as given: name all relevant axes and fields, since dataset dimensions do not expand them.

Use uniformly spaced axes with at least five points per axis for the finite-difference stencil. Any number of spatial axes can supply columns. Atomic derivative names support orders through three per axis; compound and open-form derivatives are computed during execution. For example, u_xxxx exceeds the atomic-order cap, while diff_x(u_xxx) uses composition. The fit refuses duplicate terms and target-derivative tautologies. For a second time-derivative target, set target_lhs_order=2 and use a dataset whose left-hand side is second order. The selected order must match the dataset. A first time derivative can be a feature of a second-order law; the second derivative itself, including repeated first-derivative spellings, cannot be its own predictor. Changing the target order requires a new lineage. Tabular mode refuses this setting when nondefault. A non-uniform axis or an unresolvable term fails explicitly. Smoothing noisy observations before differentiation can improve the columns used for support selection.

Tabular input selects the tabular mode. The library is then built from the table's feature columns: the constant term one first, followed by every monomial of the features from degree 1 up to degree, written as products such as mul(x, v). A terms catalog is refused on tabular data, and a non-default degree is refused on grid data, where the catalog is supplied explicitly. For ODE tables, states are the features and the derivative of one state is the target. The library contains only polynomials: a small residual on sinusoidal data can be a polynomial approximation.

The constant term is the reserved term name one, a column of ones. The tabular library always contains it, and a grid catalog can list it like any other term. Numeric literals are rejected in the term catalog in either mode; an additive constant in a law is represented as the coefficient of one. The fitted combination is restricted to the supplied columns, so a missing governing term can still produce a valid but incomplete fit.

docs.title: Method
docs.text:
KD supplies the derivatives, candidate columns and single regression target; PySINDy supplies pysindy.optimizers.STLSQ. Atomic derivative names determine the precomputed orders on each axis. Compound derivatives and open-form calls are evaluated as expressions. The finite-difference provider uses fourth-order interior stencils for first and second derivatives, with separate boundary and third-derivative stencils. In the tabular mode no derivatives are computed: the columns are one and the monomials evaluated on the feature columns, and the target is the table's target column.

STLSQ alternates a ridge solve with hard thresholding. Coefficients below threshold in magnitude are zeroed and their columns removed, until support stabilizes or max_iter rounds have run. With unbias enabled, an unregularized least-squares solve on the retained support removes ridge shrinkage. normalize_columns changes the scale at which thresholding acts, so choose normalization and threshold together.

With relative_threshold enabled, threshold is a dimensionless fraction: KD passes STLSQ the value of threshold multiplied by the L2 norm of the regression target. The setting requires normalize_columns, so STLSQ thresholds coefficients fitted on unit-norm columns, and a term is kept in a round when its coefficient times its column norm is at least threshold times the target norm. Rescaling a column or the target therefore leaves the selected support unchanged and scales the returned coefficients accordingly. With normalization and an absolute threshold, the thresholded quantity is the same product of coefficient and column norm, which carries the target's units and grows with the number of rows, so one absolute value selects differently with and without normalization and on different datasets. The norm is that of the target the optimizer receives. With a kd.Sketch, pinned terms are deducted from that target first and anchored columns are projected out of it, so the fraction refers to the part of the target that remains for STLSQ to fit.

One STLSQ solve answers the run unless the sketch hole-count step below replaces it; generations adds no further search, and the seed does not randomize the optimizer. Equivalent catalog spellings can still produce collinear numeric columns: canonical syntax catches duplicate terms but does not equate u_xx and diff2_x(u). Collinear columns can split a coefficient and change threshold selection.

A sketch with anchors or holes is checked before fitting. Each anchor must have a configured column with the same law identity. Holes admit only configured columns matching their constraints; anchors without holes leave only the anchored columns. Each hole needs at least min_count admissible distinct non-anchor law keys. A non-empty operator clause must name law features present in the library and admit an operator-bearing column as a whole; an empty clause means terminal-only. Failed checks refuse the fit.

Compilation removes pinned columns and columns sharing their jet monomials. It keeps one column per anchor and removes other spellings or columns carrying part of an anchor. Among the remaining columns, those numerically inside the anchor span are held at zero during fitting.

When there is at least one hole and summed max_count is at most 3, an empty STLSQ support or a non-anchor count outside summed min_count..max_count triggers bounded subset fitting. KD fits OLS subsets of the nonzero columns outside the anchor span, with anchors in every fit, and selects by aic_no_n (2*k + 2*ln(MSE), counting anchors and subset columns). The selected support and coefficients then come from that OLS fit, not from STLSQ thresholding. If fewer identifiable columns than summed min_count remain, STLSQ stands and the exit judges the shortfall. Above the bound of 3, STLSQ also stands and hole count is judged at exit. The compile note describes this configured rule; it does not report whether replacement ran.

docs.title: Result interpretation
docs.text:
On the ordinary path the returned coefficients are the optimizer's own. With anchors, KD solves their unpenalized coefficients by least squares; when hole-count selection replaces STLSQ, all coefficients come from KD's OLS subset fit. model.best_score_ is NMSE evaluated with the returned coefficients. model.best_expr_ lists the structural terms; read the coefficient vector on model.result_.final_eval.coefficients or the terms and coefficients on model.result_.equation. The full evaluated catalog retains zero coefficients for dropped terms and records its active support and fitted left-hand side. In the tabular mode the equation has the regression form, with the target column as its left-hand side and the selected library terms on the right. A retained one carries the additive constant as its coefficient, and the rendered equation prints that constant as a number.

Interpret NMSE with the candidate library and threshold. A small value does not establish that the library contains the governing equation. If all coefficients remain absent after the applicable fit path, the ordinary empty-support error names the threshold. An empty winning hole-count subset instead raises "hole-count selection chose the empty law"; lowering the threshold does not directly control that subset fit. Repeating an otherwise unchanged deterministic solve does not explore another structure. A near-zero residual obtained by putting the target derivative itself in the library is a tautology.

docs.title: PySR
docs.text:
Multi-population evolutionary search returning a complexity/error Pareto front.

algorithmpysrscoreNMSE mincostmediumderivativesfinite_diffequation formEVOLUTION REGRESSIONdata layoutgrid tabular

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
import kd

dataset = kd.load_burgers()
config = kd.PySRConfig(
    terms=("u", "u_x", "u_xx"), niterations=40, seed=0,
    unary_operators=("sin", "cos", "exp", "log"),
    extra_pysr_kwargs={"deterministic": True, "parallelism": "serial"},
)
model = kd.Model(algorithm="pysr", config=config)
model.fit(dataset)
print(model.result_.equation)

All fields of PySRConfig Field Type Default terms tuple[str, ...] ('u', 'u_x', 'u_xx', 'mul(u, u_x)') seed int 0 niterations int 40 population_size int 33 populations int 15 maxsize int 20 binary_operators tuple[str, ...] ('+', '-', '*', '/') unary_operators tuple[str, ...] () extra_pysr_kwargs dict[str, Any] \| None None target_lhs_order int 1

docs.title: Search space
docs.text:
PySR is a third-party symbolic-regression package whose search is documented by its authors. Its backend uses Julia. The KD wrapper supplies numeric columns and converts the result into KD's equation representation.

For PDE data, terms names the candidate columns in KD's function-call notation. PySR combines those columns but does not differentiate or invent another input column. Use the field and axis names in the dataset; supplied terms are used as given, and adding an axis does not expand them. An unresolvable term fails the fit. Compound derivatives use u_x_t or diff_t(u_x), not u_xt.

For a second time-derivative target, set target_lhs_order=2 and use a dataset whose left-hand side is second order. The selected order must match the dataset; the search does not choose between time orders. Terms that directly spell the selected target are refused, including repeated first derivatives that spell a second derivative. A first time derivative remains an admissible feature for a second-order target. Changing the target order requires a new lineage. Tabular mode refuses this setting when nondefault.

Tabular data selects tabular mode, where feature columns supply the inputs automatically and terms is refused. Grids other than one-field u with spatial axes x, y or both require explicit terms. Both modes read binary_operators and unary_operators from the configuration. These operators let the search form nonlinear combinations beyond a linear fit of the original columns.

docs.title: Method
docs.text:
KD executes the term columns into a Theta matrix and gives PySR generated placeholder names such as c0 and c1 that do not collide with dataset fields or term symbols. PySR performs its own multi-population search and returns a hall of fame with complexity, loss and expressions. One KD run contains one batch search, rather than one KD iteration per internal PySR generation. generations sets PySR's internal iteration budget.

For PDEs, conversion replaces placeholders with the terms' SymPy expressions, expands the sum, removes each additive term's numeric factor and serializes the remaining structure to KD IR. A nonzero pure-constant additive term becomes the constant term one, a column of ones, so a selected expression that is a nonzero constant becomes the law one. A fitted constant inside a unary operation, as in sin(mul(2, u)), remains part of that structure. For tables the expression stays whole, including fitted constants and additive intercepts, and an expression with no feature symbols is rejected as a constant model.

A resumed run restores PySR populations and the hall of fame and runs the new model's generations as additional internal iterations. It incurs another Julia startup. The hall of fame retains its best internal loss, while the headline expression is selected again and its KD score can move in either direction. The parameter table gives the declared resume tiers; changes to the input columns or operator vocabulary change the search identity.

docs.title: Result interpretation
docs.text:
model.best_score_ is KD's least-squares refit NMSE, not PySR's selection loss. For PDEs, the refit supplies coefficients for the converted structural terms; best_expr_ itself is structural. A retained one carries the additive constant as its refit coefficient. For tables, PySR's fitted constants remain inside the expression and the refit supplies one outer scale. That scale is often near one, but the score measures the scaled expression's shape. Refit coefficients are available on result_.final_eval.coefficients and result_.equation.

model.result_.pareto_front() returns each convertible hall-of-fame entry with its expression, PySR complexity and loss, and, for tables, its fitted outer scale. Recorder series include pareto_complexity, pareto_loss, pareto_nmse and pareto_expressions, plus pareto_scale for tables. pareto_nmse is KD's independent re-score of each entry. PySR selects the headline expression before KD re-scores it; the KD re-score does not select a new headline. Unconvertible front rows are omitted, but an unconvertible selected expression fails the run.

Code: MilesCranmer/PySR

Implementation notes. KD calls the published PySR package and targets its 1.5 API: the complexity, loss and sympy_format columns in equations_, and model.sympy() for the selected expression. It does not reimplement the search. The wrapper changes the input columns, reported score and, for PDEs, additive coefficients. Configured operators must have a KD IR representation; a custom operator or ^ can make conversion fail.

Additional backend settings pass through extra_pysr_kwargs. The timeout_in_seconds exception takes the smaller of the configured timeout and the deadline-derived bound when a deadline exists; without a deadline, the configured value is preserved (or there is no timeout if it is absent). A seed sets random_state; bitwise repeatability also needs PySR's deterministic=True and serial execution. A resumed search retains the backend's state rather than starting a fresh seeded population.

docs.text:
A genetic search over expression trees; the coefficients come from the algorithm's own sparse regression.

algorithmsgascoreAIC mincostmediumderivativesfinite_diff autogradequation formEVOLUTION REGRESSIONdata layoutgrid tabular

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
import kd

dataset = kd.load_kdv()
model = kd.Model(algorithm="sga", generations=200, seed=42)
model.fit(dataset)
print(model.result_.equation)

All fields of SGAConfig Field Type Default num int 20 p_var float 0.5 p_mute float 0.3 p_cro float 0.5 p_rep float 1.0 seed int 0 depth int 4 width int 5 aic_ratio float 1.0 lam float 0.0 d_tol float 1.0 maxit int 10 str_iters int 10 normalize int 2 dedup_mode DedupMode pre_prune use_autograd bool False field_model FieldModel \| None None autograd_train_epochs int 1000 autograd_train_lr float 0.001 autograd_train_patience int \| None None autograd_train_val_ratio float 0.0 training_dtype TrainingDtype \| None None restart_interval int \| None None functions tuple[str, ...] () constants tuple[float, ...] () target_lhs_order int 1

docs.title: Search space
docs.text:
In its PDE modes, SGA constructs an equation from expression trees over field values, spatial coordinates and derivatives. It fits coefficients during the search and needs no candidate-term library. A candidate has at most width searched trees plus the field itself, which is always included as a default column; the fitted law can therefore contain width + 1 terms. A law containing only that field is a valid outcome, while an empty law is excluded.

The finite-difference and autograd modes accept target_lhs_order=1 (the default) or 2, matching the dataset's declared target. Order 2 fits the second time derivative directly. Tabular mode refuses a nondefault PDE target order. Changing the target order starts a new lineage.

The left-hand-side axis is excluded from derivative denominators, precomputed terminals and coordinate leaves. The search space contains spatial derivatives and explicit spatial dependence. Mixed space-time derivatives, time derivatives on the right-hand side and explicit time dependence require a different grammar. A term that still differentiates along the left-hand-side axis is discarded during execution. A derivative terminal that cannot be computed is removed from the run's vocabulary with a warning.

With autograd enabled, a field surrogate is trained before the search. It supplies the first-order derivative terminals; raw field leaves still come from the observations, and derivative operators inside trees still use SGA's finite differences. Surrogate training adds a separate cost before the first generation. SGA needs no optional package, pretrained weights or endpoint.

The tabular mode searches expressions over the feature columns, the constant one and two optional vocabulary fields. functions adds unary functions, any of sin, cos, exp, log and sqrt; constants adds numeric leaves, which must be finite, distinct and different from 0 and 1. Both are empty by default, which leaves arithmetic, squares, cubes and rational expressions; the PDE modes refuse a non-empty value of either. The target column is excluded from candidates, and no field column is prepended automatically. Bare features and one can be complete terms; spatial derivative operators are absent.

A candidate containing an algebraically identically zero term or subexpression, including a zero denominator, is rejected. This also excludes zero expressions whose protected numerical values could be amplified by fitted coefficients. The rule concerns the expression itself, not a variable denominator that happens to vanish at an observed sample. A function whose argument holds no input feature after rational reduction, such as log(one), sin(6.283185307179586) or cos(div(x, x)), makes the whole tree inadmissible. Its value is a number: log(one) is zero, and the sin example is about 1e-16, which protected division turns into a large column. Offspring refused by these rules are dropped before scoring on the staged search path, so they enter neither the offspring statistics nor the evaluation count. The compatibility evaluation path reports them as invalid. Initial draws refused by them are drawn again; when 500 draws for one population slot are refused, initialization stops with an error that names the vocabulary. A vocabulary with many constants and few features can reach that bound.

Before fitting a table, SGA cancels common algebraic factors and expands polynomial roots into independently fitted monomial columns. Reduced rational roots remain whole columns, with their numerator and denominator scales normalized. Exact duplicate or linearly dependent functions are removed without using correlations between sampled values. The existing width bounds both the number of searched trees and the number of independent fitted columns; a candidate exceeding the latter bound is rejected before fitting.

A function node enters this reduction as one symbol named by its reduced argument. The argument is brought to lowest terms, with a primitive integer denominator whose first term is positive, and keeps its rational multiple, because no fitted coefficient outside the function can absorb it: sin(mul(x, x)) and sin(n2(x)) are one column, while sin(add(x, x)) and sin(x) are two, as are exp(sub(one, x)) and exp(sub(x, one)). Repeated symbols are recognized, so sub(sin(x), sin(x)) is a zero subexpression and mul(sin(x), sin(x)) is the square of one symbol. Identities between functions are not recognized: sin(x)**2 + cos(x)**2 keeps both squares as columns, and mul(exp(x), exp(y)) and exp(add(x, y)) are different symbols. Columns that agree in value without being algebraically equal are left to STRidge's column normalization and threshold.

Each table constant enters the reduction as the exact rational value of its float, so equal floats give one column. In the polynomial part of a term a constant folds into a monomial's coefficient, which the fitted coefficient absorbs: mul(2.5, x) and x are one column. A constant changes the basis only inside a function argument or in a denominator that does not cancel, as in sin(mul(2.5, x)) or div(one, add(one, mul(2.5, x))). Constants are not fitted; a value outside the table is reachable only through arithmetic of table values and one within the depth bound. pi and e enter as their float values.

The canonical columns define both numerical fitting and the returned equation. Cancellation extends removable factors to their simplified values: x/x becomes one, including at x=0. Denominators that remain after cancellation use protected division, which adds 1e-10 with the sign of the denominator, so they stay finite at their zeros; squares and cubes clamp their argument to [-1e6, 1e6]. The functions use their ordinary definitions, not the protected exp and log of KD's default registry: a column that is not finite on the table, such as log or sqrt of a negative value or an exp that overflows, is removed and the candidate's other columns are fitted. Genetic operations continue to act on the original trees.

For ODE discovery, prepare time derivatives before fitting the table. KD's trajectory preprocessing computes finite differences separately on each trajectory, or fits one multi-output neural network per trajectory and obtains time derivatives by automatic differentiation. Neural preprocessing can keep observed states as the features or use the network's state predictions; both choices share the same derivative targets. Each state equation is a separate scalar fit using all state features and any supplied trajectory parameters. Prepared tables can be reused across targets, algorithms and search seeds. Neural training belongs to preprocessing and is not repeated by a tabular search, checkpoint resume or restart. PDE surrogate settings are therefore refused when fitting a table; configure neural derivatives in preprocessing.

docs.title: Method
docs.text:
A population contains candidate equations, each a set of up to width trees of depth at most depth. In the PDE modes, leaves include every field, spatial coordinates and each field's first-order derivatives along every non-target axis. Only the left-hand-side field is prepended as the default regression column. Internal nodes are addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, square, cube and the first- and second-derivative operators. Tree roots exclude addition and subtraction because the term list already represents a sum. In tabular mode, leaves are the feature columns, one and the configured constants, and internal nodes are the same operators without the derivative operators. The configured functions join the operator, root and unary-mutation pools and the constants join the leaf pool, each in the order given, so reordering functions or constants changes the random draws. A constant is never a tree root.

Each generation applies crossover, evaluation and truncation, then mutation and replacement followed by another evaluation and truncation. Duplicate expressions are filtered by their expression keys. The evaluator uses searched trees plus the default field column in PDE modes, and canonical columns in tabular mode. It removes non-finite and all-zero columns and fits coefficients with an internal STRidge tolerance sweep. An OLS baseline is followed by adaptive d_tol steps, bounded by maxit, with str_iters ridge iterations and column normalization of order 2. The fit's AIC ranks candidates for selection. One generation is one KD iteration, controlled by generations.

With a sketch, the sum of the holes' min_count must fit within width plus one if the default field column is retained; otherwise compilation refuses the search. Anchored terms take no width: each anchored column is in every fit and is never thresholded, and a sketch with anchored terms and no hole is refused. After fitting, the selected support is aggregated by signed law key, zero and below-threshold coefficients are excluded, and anchor columns are reserved away from holes. Each remaining key occupies the first admitting hole; exceeding any hole's max_count rejects the candidate, although hole_count is declared exit_checked. Pin reservation excludes shared jet monomials but does not cover every rational respelling or a sum of separately admitted terms that reconstructs a pinned column; the compile notes describe that boundary.

In tabular mode, every tolerance comparison and candidate score uses only the selected terms. The same coefficients define the returned equation, prediction and residuals, including selected terms with small coefficients. This mode uses the existing STRidge solver and activity threshold. Its AIC term count is the number of selected canonical columns, including a selected constant; table constants are structural choices and are not counted. The AIC formula takes max(MSE, F) in place of the MSE, with F = max(tiny, (64 * n * eps)**2 * mean(y**2)) for n rows, target column y and the float64 tiny and eps, so an exact fit on noise-free data has a finite score. There is no lower AIC bound in this mode, and a support with at least as many selected columns as rows is invalid. A support in which two selected columns differ only in numeric literals, such as cos(mul(1.5, x)) and cos(mul(0.5, x)), is also invalid: the REGRESSION equation identifies a term by its structure without literals and cannot hold both. Without functions or constants this concerns rational columns such as div(one, add(2, x)) and div(one, add(3, x)). Exact algebraic compilation adds search cost and is reused through a bounded structural cache.

With restart_interval set to k, the population is re-drawn once k generations have been committed since the last draw. The re-draw happens when the next generation's proposal starts, so no draw follows the last generation and a value of at least generations leaves the run unchanged; generations remains the total across segments, and initial draws are not counted as evaluations. Restart j (j = 1, 2, ...) re-seeds the random generator with seed + 1000 * j, clears the history of expressions already seen, and draws a new population as at the start of a run. Before each re-draw, the best-ranked candidate of the finished segment replaces the stored best of earlier segments only if its AIC is strictly lower. The reported equation is the better of the stored best and the current population's best-ranked candidate, with ties going to the earlier segment. With finite differences, each segment reproduces an independent run of k generations at its seed. With autograd, the field surrogate trained before the first generation is shared by all segments, so the segments are not independent runs at those seeds. A checkpoint resume or fork trains the surrogate again from seed unless a trained surrogate is injected; changing the seed can therefore change that surrogate.

docs.title: Result interpretation
docs.text:
model.best_score_ combines fit error and support size through 2 * k * aic_ratio + 2 * ln(MSE), with max(MSE, F) in tabular mode (see Method). PDE candidates with AIC below -100 are invalid; -100 itself is valid. NMSE alone therefore does not determine which candidate is preferred. AIC ranks candidates on the same dataset; NMSE is measured on SGA's own fitting domain. For a PDE this is its grid and derivative basis, which can differ from a refit using another derivative provider. For a table it is the fixed target column and the selected observed or surrogate state features. Low training residuals alone do not establish ODE recovery; the coefficients and trajectories generated by the complete discovered system also need evaluation on independent initial conditions.

model.best_expr_ carries SGA's sparse-fit coefficients. The structured terms and coefficients are also available on model.result_.equation. KD exports function-call notation: add, sub, mul, div, n2, n3, diff_<axis>(...), diff2_<axis>(...) and terminals such as u_x. Repeated and composed derivatives may have equivalent spellings, such as diff2_x(u), diff_x(u_x) and diff_x(diff_x(u)); compare their mathematical meaning rather than their text. Compound derivative terminals use underscores, such as u_x_t, rather than the ambiguous u_xt. Tabular terms can also contain the configured function names and numeric literals from the canonical reduction, written as an integer or a float.

Tabular results carry a regression equation whose left-hand side is the target column name. An ODE derivative target is still a regression column at this interface; its time-derivative provenance belongs to the prepared data artifact. The search does not infer a differential-equation form from the target's name. Checkpoints bind the mode and feature vocabulary as well as the input identity. Tabular checkpoints also bind feature order, the canonical scoring policy and the vocabulary; cached scores from an older policy cannot be resumed under a different fitted basis. Preserve the feature order when resuming a table search. A different functions or constants starts a new lineage, so a run cannot be resumed under another vocabulary.

The recorder exposes best_aic, gen_best_aic, gen_best_nmse, gen_mean_aic, gen_mean_complexity, n_valid and n_unique. The gen_* series describe newly evaluated offspring; pop_mean_aic describes the surviving population. A flat best-score curve records a lack of improvement on that run, and does not establish whether the structure is correct.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
Chen et al. (2022). "Symbolic genetic algorithm for discovering open-form partial differential equations (SGA-PDE)". Phys. Rev. Research 4, 023174. Paper · arXiv:2106.11927

Code: YuntianChen/SGA-PDE

Implementation notes. KD's SGA was ported from an earlier implementation of SGA-PDE. For PDE data, it preserves the paper's three-tree construction at the standard width and STRidge column normalization (normalize=2), with crossover pairing and the two-stage selection order checked against that implementation. Protected division keeps mixed-zero divisors finite. The tree finite-difference implementation uses a five-point fourth-order stencil, with a three-point stencil on shorter arrays, where the reference used three-point second-order differences. Non-finite MSE and fits with empty support receive infinite AIC, and so does zero MSE in the PDE modes. The tabular mode, with its function vocabulary, constant table and MSE floor, is a KD addition; the reference implementation fits PDEs only.

Only first-order derivative terminals are precomputed; higher orders come from tree composition. There is no literal-zero terminal or param_fields injection for non-differentiable parameter fields. The term executor and data layer have different boundary stencils, so a precomputed derivative and its tree-composed equivalent can differ at boundaries.

docs.title: Worked example
docs.text:
The run below uses the KdV dataset that ships with KD: a 256 × 201 grid whose cosine initial condition steepens under the nonlinear term and then breaks into a train of solitary waves that separate at different speeds, the tallest of them reaching an amplitude of 2.3.

The observed field over its physical spatial and time coordinates.

Running the snippet above, model.best_expr_ is:

SGA-PDE · kdv · seed 42 generation 200 / 200 · nmse 2.70e-06 · AIC -19.42 \(u_t =\)\(-u\,u_x\)\(-0.0025\,u_{xxx}\) Equation Discovered \(u_t = -u\,u_x -0.0025\,u_{xxx}\) Reference \(u_t = -u\,u_x -0.0025\,u_{xxx}\)

Both terms and both coefficients match. The search was not narrowed to them: SGA-PDE was given no candidate library, so the two terms were assembled from operators during the run, and the two coefficients came from its own sparse regression rather than from a fit against the answer.

The fitted derivative target, its equation prediction, and predicted minus measured values. The first two panels share a color scale; the residual has its own scale, with any clipping disclosed on the figure.

docs.title: API reference
docs.text:
This reference covers KD's dataset, model, result and analysis entry points, with signatures and parameters from the library. Common entry points are imported from kd, including kd.Model and kd.load_kdv. Batch execution, surrogate transport and plugin interfaces also expose names through kd.harness, kd.models and kd.search; each page gives the import location.

Descriptions come from the library's own docstrings, cut to reference length. Where a parameter carries more than a sentence of contract, the guide pages in the user guide and design documentation explain it: resume tiers in Parameter tiers and resuming, what the scores mean in Score conventions, term syntax in Equation representation.

Once kd.Model(config=...) receives one it is the single source of that algorithm's settings, and passing the same settings as kd.Model keywords alongside it raises. docs.title: register_algorithm
docs.text:
register_algorithm(
    name: str, plugin_cls: type[FacadeWiringContract]
) -> None

Register plugin_cls as the algorithm name.

Raises:

  • ValueError –

    name does not match [a-z][a-z0-9_]* or is registered already; plugin_cls.descriptor.algorithm is not name; constructor_kwargs names a keyword other than mode, task, surrogate_model and provider.

  • TypeError –

    The constructor takes no keyword that constructor_kwargs names; config_cls has no seed field; the descriptor declares config_artifact_keys and the class lacks train_surrogate or artifacts.

    *,
    topology: str,
