docs.title: Real-world measurements
docs.text:
Two datasets of laboratory measurements ship alongside the benchmarks. Both are tables of observations rather than fields on a regular grid, so they load as kd.TabularDataset and are not entries of the catalog above.

kd.load_tlc_cc() holds 74 rows from an automated column-chromatography platform, which separated 192 organic compounds on 4 g silica columns with thin-layer chromatography giving the retardation factor of each compound and eluent pair. Each row is one experimental condition rather than one compound: the features are the retardation factor R_F and the petroleum-ether fraction r of the eluent, and the target is the retention volume averaged over the compounds run at that condition, either the volume at which a compound is first detected (target="start") or the volume at which it has fully eluted (target="end").

kd.load_wave_breaking() holds surface-elevation measurements from the 27.2 m glass-walled wave tank at Imperial College London: focused wave groups propagating toward breaking, with the air-water interface reconstructed frame by frame from three cameras running at 20 Hz. The features are the time t and the position x along the tank; the target is the surface elevation eta. The points are scattered rather than gridded, and the three camera windows do not overlap, so x covers three disjoint intervals. One experiment of the campaign is bundled, 314,478 points, and data_dir= points the loader at the others.

Both datasets are published measurements, used with the permission of the authors: the chromatography platform in Xu, Wu, Chen, Zhang and Mo, Nat Commun 16, 832 (2025), and the wave-tank campaigns in Xu, Chen, Cao, Tang, Du, Li, Callaghan and Zhang, Nat Commun 16, 10255 (2025). Breaking waves is a worked run on the wave data.

docs.title: Derivative sources
docs.text: For PDE discovery, KD computes derivatives from observed field values using finite differences on a grid or automatic differentiation through a neural network that represents the field. Tabular regression fits a target column without derivatives.

docs.title: Finite differences
docs.text:
Central-difference stencils applied directly on the grid. Every derivative is computed once before the search starts, and every later use is a lookup.

  • First- and second-order derivatives use fourth-order accurate stencils; third-order uses a second-order accurate one. Atomic derivatives are supported up to third order.
  • Periodic axes use a wrap-around stencil, so boundary points keep the interior accuracy; non-periodic axes fall back to reduced-order formulas at the boundary.
  • Coordinates must be increasing and evenly spaced.

kd.derivative_field(dataset, field, axis, order=1, *, derivatives="finite_diff") returns one derivative of one field of a grid dataset, on the dataset's own grid and with the field's shape. It builds the provider a search is given ("finite_diff", or "fd2" for the three-point second-order profile) on the complete dataset, so it returns the same values, bit for bit, as the target a search regresses and the terminal derivatives the search is given: kd.derivative_field(dataset, "u", "x", 2) is the search's u_xx. No boundary rows are dropped; the outermost points take the wrap-around or reduced-order formulas described above. To see a derivative after smoothing, pass the smoothed copy of the dataset, for example kd.lowpass_smooth(dataset, modes=32). The function trains no network, so it refuses derivatives="autograd" and scattered samples, and it serves only KD's own finite-difference providers, not providers registered by an extension.

docs.title: Automatic differentiation
docs.text: A neural network is trained to map coordinates to field values, and PyTorch autograd differentiates that network. The derivatives are exact for the trained network, so they are not bounded by a stencil's order and they need not be evaluated at the original grid points. The price is one extra training run.

docs.title: Surrogate network sources
docs.text:
Three things can supply the network that gets differentiated:

  • Trained by the platform: an algorithm declares that it needs a surrogate network, and the platform trains one and wires it in with nothing required from you. This is DLGA-PDE's route.
  • Trained by the algorithm: under derivatives="autograd", SGA-PDE trains its own surrogate network and uses it for the terminal derivatives (u_x, u_t), while derivative operators inside the expression tree still go through the dataset's finite differences.
  • Supplied by you: kd.Model(algorithm="dlga", surrogate_model=...) takes an already-trained torch.nn.Module and the platform skips its own training. The parameter applies to DLGA-PDE only.

docs.title: Derivative source per algorithm
docs.text:
Every mode of every algorithm declares its derivative source in kd.instrument_schemas():

import kd

for schema in kd.instrument_schemas():
    for mode in schema["modes"]:
        print(f"{schema['algorithm']:9s} {mode['name']:15s} {mode['provider_kind']}")

sga       default         finite_diff
sga       autograd        autograd
sga       tabular         none
dlga      default         autograd
discover  mode1           finite_diff
discover  mode2           autograd
discover  tabular         none
pysr      default         finite_diff
pysr      tabular         none
eqgpt     single_wave     finite_diff
eqgpt     wave_multicase  none
eqgpt     steady          none
llm4ed    default         finite_diff
llm4ed    tabular         none
pysindy   default         finite_diff
pysindy   tabular         none

DLGA-PDE differentiates through a network. The PDE modes of DISCOVER, PySR and PySINDy use finite differences, as do LLM4ED and EqGPT's single-case wave mode; SGA-PDE offers both and defaults to finite differences. DISCOVER, PySR and PySINDy also have tabular regression modes, which fit a target column without derivatives and report none. EqGPT's multi-case wave mode and steady mode report none: they take no derivatives from the platform and build their own field representation and evaluation internally.

docs.title: Configurable options
docs.text:
• How SGA-PDE differentiates: kd.Model(algorithm="sga", derivatives="autograd") switches the terminal derivatives to autograd. On a regular, well-resolved grid the default finite differences are computed once and cost you no training run; choose autograd when you want the derivatives to come from a continuous representation of the field.
  • DLGA-PDE's surrogate network: by default the platform trains it from the surrogate settings in kd.DLGAConfig. If you already have a trained field network, pass it through surrogate_model= and that training is skipped.

The other modes have a fixed derivative source. For what the data itself must look like, see data requirements.

docs.title: Data requirements
docs.text: KD reads a set of observations and searches for the equation behind them. For field data that means two things: a set of coordinate axes, and one or more fields sampled on those coordinates. Scalar regression data is a plain X -> y table instead, and carries no axes at all. The derivatives, the candidate terms and the coefficients are all produced by the algorithm.

docs.title: Build a dataset from arrays
docs.text:
kd.PDEDataset.from_arrays wraps arrays you already have. The key order of coords fixes the axis order, and each field array must have exactly the shape given by the axis lengths in that order.

import numpy as np
import kd

x = np.linspace(0.0, 2 * np.pi, 128, endpoint=False)   # periodic axis, endpoint not repeated
t = np.linspace(0.0, 1.0, 64)
u = np.sin(x)[:, None] * np.exp(-t)[None, :]      # shape (128, 64)

dataset = kd.PDEDataset.from_arrays(
    coords={"x": x, "t": t},
    fields={"u": u},
    lhs="u_t",
    periodic={"x"},
    name="my-data",
)

kd.preview(dataset)

Dataset: my-data
Axes:
     x | n=128  | range [0.000, 6.234] | step 0.04909 (uniform)
     t | n=64   | range [0.000, 1.000] | step 0.01587 (uniform)
Fields:
     u | dtype=float64 | shape=(128, 64) | min=-1.000 max=1.000 mean=0.000 (NaN=0)
LHS: u_t  (field='u', axis='t')
Status: ready to fit

That dataset goes straight into kd.Model.fit(). kd.preview prints, per axis, the point count, range and whether the step is uniform; per field, the dtype, shape, extrema and NaN count; plus the left-hand side it parsed. kd.preview_report returns the same facts as an object you can read from code. It also gives, for each field and each uniformly spaced axis with at least five points, a noise estimate relative to the field's standard deviation and two finite-difference consistency measures that compare central differences with step 1 and step 2 for the first and second derivatives. They are the noise_estimate, first_derivative_gap and second_derivative_gap dictionaries of each FieldReport, keyed by axis name. kd.preview does not print these three values.

kd.Model(savgol_window=w) smooths every field of a grid dataset along every axis with a Savitzky-Golay filter of window length w and polynomial order 3 before the search starts, for any algorithm; Model.train_surrogate trains on the same smoothed data, and the default 0 leaves the data unchanged. kd.data.savgol_smooth(dataset, w) returns the smoothed copy as a new dataset, so its effect can be inspected with kd.preview_report before a fit.

Two methods return a modified copy of a grid dataset and leave the original unchanged. dataset.with_field("u", values) replaces one field with an array of the same shape, converted to that field's dtype and device. dataset.window("t", stop=0.5) keeps the points whose coordinate on that axis lies in the inclusive range from start to stop (either bound may be left open) and slices every field the same way; a periodic axis that the window cuts is no longer marked periodic. Both copies keep the left-hand side, the other axes and fields, and the dataset's source. A scattered or tabular dataset raises.

docs.title: Load a dataset from a file
docs.text:
kd.load takes a catalog id or a file path. A catalog id returns that entry (kd.load("kdv") is kd.load_kdv()). A path is read on evidence, never on a guess: a registered layout that recognizes the file's arrays builds the dataset, otherwise you name the arrays yourself, or you pass a loader function of your own. kd.inspect_file lists every array first (key, shape, dtype, finite range and NaN/Inf counts), so the mapping can be written from what the file holds. Its layouts attribute names the registered layouts that recognize the file; an empty list means kd.load needs coords= and fields=.

A file holds one of three kinds of data, and kd.load decides which before it reads any value. kind="pde", kind="trajectory" or kind="tabular" states it. Without kind, coords that map only t, with fields naming every state variable, read a kd.data.TrajectorySet (see ODE trajectories); an lhs that names a column, without coords, reads a kd.TabularDataset (see Tabular data); anything else is a grid PDEDataset, read by the rules in the rest of this section. A grid records the file it came from in dataset.source, a trajectory set or a table in file_source.

import kd

report = kd.inspect_file("heat.npz")
print(report.layouts)   # ['plain-grid'] for t, x and a field of shape (len(x), len(t))

dataset = kd.load("heat.npz")   # plain-grid layout, no options
dataset = kd.load("1D_Burgers_Sols_Nu0.01.hdf5", select={"sample": 0})   # pdebench-1d layout
dataset = kd.load("run.mat", coords={"x": "x", "t": "tt"}, fields={"u": "usol"}, lhs="u_t")
dataset = kd.load("run.bin", loader=read_my_format)   # your function returns a PDEDataset

The registered layouts are:

  • pdebench-1d and pdebench-cfd: PDEBench HDF5 files. A file with several samples needs select={"sample": i}.
  • kd-npz: an .npz holding axis_order, one coordinate array per axis and the field arrays.
  • kd-scattered-npz: an .npz whose scalar format entry is kd-scattered-npz-v1. It holds axis_order, field_names, and one per-point vector coord__<axis> or field__<name> for each axis and field, and builds a scattered dataset.
  • plain-grid: an .npz or a MATLAB file (v5 or v7.3) with a time array t and at least one of x, y, z, each a 1-D, row or column vector. Every other array except 0-d scalars is a field; the fields keep their stored names, share one shape with one dimension per coordinate, and the axis order is read from the dimension lengths. When two coordinates have the same length, kd.load raises and names the explicit call with field_axes=.

The order of a coords= mapping is the axis order of the dataset. Without field_axes=, kd.load reads each field's storage order from its dimension lengths, as the plain-grid layout does, and transposes the field into mapping order. When two mapped coordinates have the same length, the lengths cannot give the storage order, so kd.load raises and its message gives the calls with field_axes= that state it: field_axes=["x", "t"] when u[i, j] is the value at x[i] and t[j], field_axes=["t", "x"] when it is the value at t[i] and x[j]. A field with a sample axis names that axis in field_axes= and picks one sample with select=. Periodicity is never in a file: state it with periodic={"x"}.

A CSV file with a header row is read without a layout, one point per row. Without mappings, the field named by lhs is the only field and every other column is a coordinate, in header order; coords= and fields= select named columns instead. A complete set of unique coordinate combinations is pivoted to a grid, whose axes must be evenly spaced; any other set of points stays scattered. An .xlsx workbook needs coords= and fields= naming its column headers and is read through kd.PDEDataset.from_xlsx.

The layout and mapping routes end in from_arrays (or from_scatter for scattered data), and the dataset carries source (path, sha256, container, layout, hints) so a program can see where it came from; it stays out of the dataset fingerprint and out of run records.

docs.title: Axis and field requirements
docs.text:
• Any number of axes is accepted. The coords mapping fixes both the count and the order, and each field array carries one dimension per axis. The example above has one spatial axis and time; kd.load_burgers_2d() is a bundled dataset with two spatial axes and time, and lap(u) sums the second derivative over whichever spatial axes the dataset has. Which layouts a given algorithm accepts is declared per algorithm and checked at fit() (see below).
  • Each axis is a 1-D increasing array: a decreasing coordinate is rejected by from_arrays itself, at construction.
  • Axes are evenly spaced. Finite-difference stencils are written around a fixed step, so an unevenly spaced axis is rejected when the derivatives are taken (algorithms that differentiate a trained surrogate instead are not bound by this).
  • Fields are floating-point arrays with no NaN and no Inf. from_arrays casts coordinates and fields to float64 by default.
  • Axis names are free-form strings, but derivative symbols (u_xx) are parsed against single-letter axis names, so x, y, t save you trouble.
  • periodic marks the axes with periodic boundaries: they are differentiated with a wrap-around stencil, so boundary points keep the interior accuracy. Do not repeat the endpoint on a periodic axis (use [0, L), not [0, L]).

docs.title: The left-hand side
docs.text:
lhs spells out the term on the left of the equation using KD's derivative naming convention; KD parses the field, the axis and the order out of it.

  • lhs="u_t" (default): first-order in time, i.e. u_t = f(u, u_x, u_xx, ...). Most algorithms target this form. kd.load takes the single field's name instead when a grid has one field, so a MATLAB file whose field is usol loads with lhs="usol_t".
  • lhs="u_tt": second order. The bundled wave and klein-gordon datasets are of this kind. DLGA, PySR, PySINDy, SGA (finite differences or autograd), and DISCOVER (MODE1 or MODE2) accept this target with target_lhs_order=2 in their configs. DLGA also provides kd.DLGAConfig.wave_preset() / kd.DLGAConfig.kg_preset() for these datasets. Check the selected mode's lhs_orders in kd.instrument_schemas() for other algorithms; an unsupported order is rejected at fit().
  • A steady problem has no time derivative and therefore no left-hand side: build it with kd.PDEDataset.from_scatter(..., lhs="") and the equation reads as a sum of terms equal to zero. The three bundled Laplace / Poisson datasets are of this kind.

docs.title: Scattered points
docs.text:
Data that does not sit on a regular grid goes through kd.PDEDataset.from_scatter: every coordinate array and every field array is a 1-D array of length N, one entry per observed point, and the coordinates need not be sorted. kd.PDEDataset.from_xlsx reads the same structure directly out of an xlsx workbook by column header, which fits experimental data already stored as (x, y, u) columns.

Scattered data is handled by EqGPT: its multi-case wave mode and its steady mode declare scattered.

docs.title: Tabular data
docs.text:
A scalar regression task is a plain X -> y table, and kd.TabularDataset carries one: X is an array of shape (n_samples, n_features), y is a (n_samples,) array of the measured target, var_names gives one name per column of X, and target_name names y. There are no coordinate axes: a row is one observation, not a sample of a field. name, source and description record where the table came from, and are required alongside the four above.

import numpy as np
import kd

pressure = np.linspace(1.0, 5.0, 40)
flow = np.linspace(0.2, 2.0, 40)

table = kd.TabularDataset(
    X=np.column_stack([pressure, flow]),
    y=2.0 * pressure + 3.0,
    var_names=("pressure", "flow"),
    target_name="reactor_yield",
    name="my-table",
    source="lab notebook",
    description="reactor yield against pressure and flow rate",
)

fit() reads the table through one converter, and that is where the names and the values are checked: every name is a Python identifier, distinct from the others, and neither a Python keyword nor one of the names KD reserves for its own functions, derivatives and the constant term one; every value is finite; the columns are read as float64.

That table goes straight into kd.Model.fit(). Each column becomes a field of its own and the target column becomes the left-hand side. No derivatives are taken, so a column named x or t is just another feature. The result is an expression in the feature names rather than a PDE. result_.lhs_label is the target column, and best_expr_ carries the expression together with the constants fitted for it. An algorithm whose tabular mode declares the REGRESSION form returns the same answer on result_.equation as well, the target column on the left of it.

SGA, DISCOVER, PySR, LLM4ED and PySINDy read this layout: each declares a tabular mode, and KD selects that mode from the dataset you hand to fit(). On a table, the reserved term one is a column of ones with the length of the target column. PySINDy's tabular library starts with one, followed by every monomial of the feature columns up to PySINDyConfig.degree, so an additive constant in the fitted law is the coefficient of one and is printed as a number in result_.equation. KD ships one table of its own, kd.load_tlc_cc(), which returns a TabularDataset ready to fit.

kd.load(path, lhs="y") reads a table from a CSV or XLSX file with a header row, or from an .npz or MATLAB file of column vectors: the column y is the target and every other column is an input, in file order; fields= selects and renames columns and must include the target.

kd.load_tabular(path) reads a table stored as an .npz whose scalar format entry is kd-tabular-npz-v1, with the arrays X, y, var_names and target_name, and returns a TabularDataset whose names and values have passed the checks above.

docs.title: ODE trajectories
docs.text: Time series of an ordinary differential equation system are held in a kd.data.TrajectorySet rather than in a dataset. kd.load(path, coords={"t": "t"}, fields={"x": "x", "y": "y"}) reads one from a file: coords maps only the time variable, fields maps every state in state order, trajectory_id= names the column that tells several trajectories apart in one table, and params= maps constant parameters per trajectory. The time grid may be non-uniform. Model.fit does not take a trajectory set: each trajectory is differentiated separately and the result is projected to one regression table per target state, as described under ODE trajectories.

docs.title: Supported layouts per algorithm
docs.text:
Every mode of every algorithm declares the layouts it accepts (topologies: grid / scattered / tabular) and the equation forms it searches (forms: EVOLUTION / HOMOGENEOUS / REGRESSION, or empty for a mode that returns a bare expression) in kd.instrument_schemas(); the spec strip at the top of each algorithm page shows the same information. When the layout or the left-hand-side order of your data does not match the algorithm, fit() raises and names what that algorithm does support.

To try an algorithm before pointing it at your own data, start from the bundled datasets. For how the derivatives are produced, see derivative sources.

docs.title: ODE trajectories
docs.text: kd.data.TrajectorySet groups time series with the same state and parameter names. Each Trajectory carries its own strictly increasing time array, state values and known parameter values; trajectories may have different lengths or nonuniform sampling. Model.fit takes a PDEDataset or a TabularDataset, not a trajectory set. The preparation below differentiates each trajectory separately and projects the result to one regression table per target state, which Model.fit then takes like any other table.

docs.title: Build a trajectory set
docs.text:
A set is constructed from Trajectory objects, or generated for one of the systems in kd.data.ODE_SYSTEMS. generate_ode_trajectories integrates n_trajectories trajectories from initial states drawn with the given seed:

from kd.data import generate_ode_trajectories

trajectories = generate_ode_trajectories("van_der_pol", seed=0)
trajectories.state_vars   # ('x', 'v')

docs.title: Prepare regression tables
docs.text:
Prepare derivatives separately on each trajectory before concatenating regression rows:

from kd import Model
from kd.data import prepare_trajectory_regression

# trajectories is a TrajectorySet containing the observed states.
prepared = prepare_trajectory_regression(trajectories, derivatives="finite_diff")
table = prepared.table(trajectories.state_vars[0], state_source="observed", trim=2)
model = Model("sga", generations=200, seed=0).fit(table)

The columns contain all states followed by the known parameters. The target for state x is named dx_dt. Trimming removes samples at both ends of each trajectory after differentiation, so rows from separate trajectories never share a difference stencil. The existing trajectories_to_tabular function retains its single-target finite-difference behavior and its default of no trimming.

docs.title: Use neural derivatives
docs.text:
Neural preprocessing fits one time-input, multi-output FieldModel per trajectory, then uses AutogradProvider for derivatives in the original physical units. Different initial conditions are fitted separately. The materialized result can supply either observed or network-predicted state features with the same neural derivative target:

from kd.data import TrajectoryNNConfig, prepare_trajectory_regression

prepared = prepare_trajectory_regression(
    trajectories,
    derivatives="autograd",
    nn_config=TrajectoryNNConfig(seed=0, max_epochs=5000),
)
observed = prepared.table("x", state_source="observed", trim=2)
smoothed = prepared.table("x", state_source="surrogate", trim=2)

The epoch budget above is an explicit example setting; derivative accuracy requires evaluation for the data in use. Selecting another target or state source reuses the same arrays. Finite-difference preprocessing supports observed state features only. Search parameters control the subsequent table fit; Model(..., derivatives="autograd") configures the PDE surrogate path and is not a second preprocessing stage for these tables.

docs.title: Save a preparation
docs.text: save_trajectory_regression and load_trajectory_regression store and restore the fixed numerical result, its recipe and training reports. A projection's content identity is carried in the table name and binds its target, state source, trimming and numerical values. Keep the saved preparation artifact alongside search records to retain the full recipe. Editing a projected table's values or identity invalidates that preparation binding. Neural training cost is reported once per preparation, separately from the searches that reuse it.

docs.title: KD Studio preview
docs.text:
This preview includes Burgers and KdV data, preprocessing previews and algorithm settings. Results are recorded examples. The Run button shows local setup instructions and, when available, a configuration to copy. It does not start a search.

KD Studio quick start · Quick start · KD Studio guide

The preview includes sample data and search settings. The KD Studio quick start explains installation and a first search.

Enable JavaScript to use the interactive preview, or follow the KD Studio quick start.

docs.title: Design
docs.text:
KD is a platform for discovering partial differential equations from data, organized as a set of algorithm plugins. Each plugin implements the algorithm-specific search procedure and scientific logic, while the platform provides the data processing, execution, visualization, and experiment infrastructure shared across algorithms. Seven algorithms are currently integrated: five published by our group (SGA-PDE, DLGA-PDE, DISCOVER, EqGPT, LLM4ED) and two external baselines (PySR, PySINDy).

Inputs flow into a dataset, an algorithm searches it, and a result carries the equation, the score and the run record. Platform services are used as each algorithm's declaration states. The package layers behind this view are on the Architecture page. Open the figure in a new tab for full size.

Data is prepared once and an algorithm is chosen by name:

model = kd.Model(algorithm="sga").fit(data)

The fitted model carries the equation, the score, and the record of the run. Selecting a different algorithm changes only the algorithm argument; the surrounding code and the way the result is read stay the same.

docs.title: Division of responsibility
docs.text: Algorithms own their search, scoring and final fit. Platform services are optional; each algorithm declares which services and data forms its modes use. The platform and plugin contract describes the required members, shared services and per-algorithm responsibilities.

docs.title: Shared machinery
docs.text: Datasets hold observations. Derivative providers compute derivatives from those observations or from a trained field model when requested. The data requirements and derivative sources describe these choices; optional services cover the evaluation and fitting components.

docs.title: Shared notation
docs.text: Public equations use term strings such as mul(u, u_x) and diff_x(diff2_x(u)), paired with coefficients and a left-hand side. Checkpoints preserve the plugin's native search state. Equation representation explains the term syntax, input contracts and structural comparison.

docs.title: Score comparability
docs.text: The fitted model retains the algorithm's own score. Comparisons require matching data, derivative and scoring conventions. Score conventions explains how to refit candidate terms in a shared context with kd.evaluate_terms.

docs.title: Figures from one call
docs.text: model.report renders the supported figures and an HTML report from a fitted model. Visualization explains the shared figures and algorithm-specific panels; Figure generation covers the report and individual plotting calls.

docs.title: Checkpoints and resuming
docs.text: A checkpoint restores search state; the new model supplies the configuration for the resumed segment. Parameter tiers and resuming explains the checkpoint manifest, resume-safe parameters, identity checks and branching.

docs.title: Batch studies
docs.text: Batch experiments describes ordered plans across seeds, algorithms and datasets, sealed evidence stores and consensus from the recorded results.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: The Architecture page contains the complete component diagram, package layers and conventions that cross layers. The detailed SVG can be opened at full size from that page.

docs.title: The path of one fit
docs.text: The execution sequence follows dataset construction, component assembly, search, result assembly and subsequent analysis.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
KD's packages form a layered structure in which each layer imports only the layers below it. The order is a contract checked by import-linter on every push, so a new module that is not placed in a layer, or an import that crosses the order without being declared, fails the build. The figure below shows the layers, the algorithm packages, the three conventions that cross several layers, and the order in which one call to Model.fit passes through them.

Open the full-size architecture diagram

The preview below shows the full diagram. Open the SVG to zoom in on package names, declarations and execution steps.

Bands are import layers, upper layers import lower ones, with a small number of declared exceptions. Numbers give the execution order of one fit. A dot marks a layer that takes part in the convention named above the column. Open the figure in a new tab for full size.

docs.title: Layers
docs.text:
Algorithm packages are independent of one another. Import-linter checks both the package layers and the registered algorithm packages; a newly added module must be assigned to the appropriate layer. Algorithms import visualization descriptors to declare their diagnostic panels, so the figure layer sits below the algorithm packages. Declared exceptions are shown on the diagram.

From the bottom up:

  • Leaf packages. kd.models holds the neural field model and its trainer. kd.llm holds the provider protocol, an OpenAI-compatible client, budget accounting and a request tape for replay. Neither imports any other part of KD.
  • kd.data. The dataset types, PDEDataset for fields on axes and TabularDataset for a feature matrix with a target, together with the file loaders, the dataset catalog, the derivative providers, synthetic generators, noise and subsampling. Derivatives are computed on request and never stored in a dataset.
  • kd.core. The term notation and its operator registry, the executor that turns a term string into a column of numbers, the evaluator that assembles the design matrix and calls a linear solver, the scores, the numerical guards, the equation types with their signatures and sketches, and the platform builder that resolves the left-hand side and assembles the components an algorithm declared it needs.
  • kd.viz. The figure engine, the individual plots and the HTML report. The engine reads the score metadata carried by a result and the figure descriptors each algorithm publishes through the VizExtension protocol.
  • kd.search. The framework half holds the SearchAlgorithm contract, the runner that drives prepare and then propose, evaluate and update per iteration, the per-iteration recorder, checkpoint writing with its manifest, and the result assembly. The plugin half holds one package per algorithm. Each package owns its search procedure, its scoring and its final fit, and carries its own figure extension; SGA-PDE and PySINDy also carry a sketch backend.
  • kd.api, kd.evaluate, kd.inspect. The Model facade, term evaluation without a search, equation verification, cross-algorithm comparison, dataset inspection and preview.
  • kd.harness. Batch execution: a plan of runs executed serially or in supervised child processes under resource limits, an evidence store with hashed records, merging of stores written by separate batches, and consensus across runs.

docs.title: Conventions that cross layers
docs.text:
Three conventions apply in several layers at once and are drawn as columns beside the bands.

  • Expression bus. An equation that crosses a package boundary is written as term strings such as mul(u, u_x). Each algorithm keeps its own representation inside its package, the expression tree of SGA-PDE, the token sequence of DISCOVER, the vocabulary of EqGPT, the SymPy expression of PySR, and converts on the way out. Checkpoints are the exception: a plugin's saved state keeps its native form, since it is read back only by the same plugin. See Equation representation.
  • Capability declarations. Each algorithm declares, as data on its class, the equation forms and data layouts of each mode, the source of its derivatives, the name and direction of its score, whether it answers in one shot, which parameters survive a resume, and how far each mode honours a sketch. The facade, the runner, the batch harness, the website generator and the agent controller read the same declaration; the figure engine reads its projection in the result. See Platform and plugins.
  • Checkpoint and manifest. The runner writes the plugin's own state atomically during a run and keeps a manifest of what it wrote. A resume selects an entry from that manifest and validates the stored parameters against the new configuration. See Parameter tiers and resuming.

docs.title: Execution order of one fit
docs.text:
1. A dataset is built from a file, a catalog entry or arrays, optionally with noise or subsampling applied.
  2. PlatformBuilder resolves the left-hand side, builds the derivative source the algorithm declared, and assembles the components. A mode that declares no platform derivatives receives neither a derivative provider nor an evaluator; the term executor is still available.
  3. ExperimentRunner calls prepare, then repeats propose, evaluate and update until the iteration budget or the algorithm's own stop condition ends the run, recording each iteration, calling callbacks and writing checkpoints at the configured interval when a directory was given. The algorithm owns the work within each iteration step.
  4. The algorithm builds its final evaluation and the target it was fitted against. The platform does not re-score the winning candidate.
  5. The runner assembles the Equation, when the final evaluation yields one, and the run record.
  6. model.result_ holds the ExperimentResult; model.best_expr_ and model.best_score_ expose the algorithm's expression and objective value.
  7. Reports, verification, comparison, batch aggregation and agent use are separate calls on that result. A fit with a sketch also verifies the sketch before returning.

The algorithms use different parts of the setup and evaluation services. The platform and plugin responsibilities describe their native search, fitting and surrogate components.

docs.title: Components outside the layer order
docs.text:
• Agent controller. kd-agent drives a search through a fixed set of verbs, keeps a tree of checkpoints that can be resumed, branched or pruned, and uses only the public API of KD. KD never imports the controller.
  • Website. The parameter tables and specification strips on this site are generated from the capability declarations.
  • External dependencies. PySR runs in a Python worker process that starts its Julia runtime; PySINDy contributes its STLSQ optimizer; LLM4ED reaches a language-model endpoint through kd.llm; the agent controller reaches an OpenAI-compatible or Anthropic endpoint directly; remote datasets and model weights are fetched from the Hugging Face Hub.

docs.title: Conceptual view
docs.text:
The second figure keeps the same components but groups them by role rather than by import layer. It is the view used when introducing KD.

Inputs flow into a dataset, an algorithm searches it, and a result carries the equation, the score and the run record. Platform services are used as each algorithm's declaration states; reports, verification, batch runs and the agent are separate calls on the result. Open the figure in a new tab for full size.

docs.title: Batch experiments and evidence
docs.text: A single fit covers one configuration. Answering whether a result holds at another seed, on another dataset or under another algorithm requires many runs. kd.harness runs a matrix of configurations and records each one, so the aggregate is computed from the records rather than assembled by hand.

docs.title: The experiment plan
docs.text:
An ExperimentPlan is an ordered matrix of entries, each naming an algorithm, a dataset, a seed and the settings for that run. Its hash covers the matrix including the order, so the hash identifies the exact study. Datasets are referred to by name and resolved at run time, which keeps the plan itself free of data.

import kd
from kd.harness import ExperimentPlan, PlanEntry, run_plan

dataset = kd.generate_burgers_data(nx=64, nt=32, nu=0.1, seed=0)

plan = ExperimentPlan(
    name="burgers-seed-stability",
    entries=tuple(
        PlanEntry(
            instrument="sga",
            dataset_ref="burgers",
            seed=seed,
            model_kwargs={"generations": 6, "population": 12},
        )
        for seed in (0, 1, 2)
    ),
)
print(plan.name, len(plan.entries), plan.plan_hash()[:10])

result = run_plan(plan, datasets={"burgers": dataset}, store_root="out/burgers-seeds")
for outcome in result.outcomes:
    print(outcome.entry_index, outcome.entry.instrument, outcome.entry.seed, outcome.status)

burgers-seed-stability 3 1ec66c4dac
0 sga 0 completed
1 sga 1 completed
2 sga 2 completed

Widening the study means editing those entries to add an algorithm, a dataset or more seeds. The surrounding code does not change, and the new matrix receives its own hash.

By default run_plan runs the entries one after another in the calling process, so the batch ends if that process dies, and the outcomes written before that point remain in the store. run_plan(..., parallel=kd.harness.ParallelOptions(limits=...)) runs them in supervised child processes instead: limits sets the number of process slots, GPU slots and the memory budget that admit an entry, device_by_instrument sends an algorithm's entries to "cpu" or "cuda" (each cuda child sees only its own card), and hard_seconds and memory_max_gb bound each child. The device never enters the plan or its hash. Batches that ran separately, for example on different days or machines, are combined with merge_stores: pass the stores in order, under the plan's name.

merge_stores writes a new store from several sealed ones and leaves the sources unchanged. The merged plan is the sources' entries concatenated in the order given, so a single run_plan over the same entries under the same name has the same plan hash and the same entry indices. Records are copied unchanged, and the new store is reopened and re-verified after the copy. The merge is refused when one entry was attempted in two sources, when one dataset name refers to different data in two sources, or when a source is itself a merged store. An entry counts as attempted once it has an outcome of any status, so an entry that failed in one batch and was run again in another cannot be merged back with the first batch. An entry that a batch never reached can be run in a later batch and merged.

The merged store keeps one row per source with its plan name, plan hash, entry range and environment, and its top-level environment holds only the fields on which all sources agree. When the sources ran under different KD versions or commits, the merge requires a version_note stating what changed between them and whether it affects the results. The store report then lists each source's KD version and commit together with the note. The consensus report lists them as well when it is rendered with the merged store, render_consensus_markdown(report, store=merged).

docs.title: Failed entries
docs.text: An entry that raises is recorded with its error type and message, and the remaining entries still run. Each outcome carries one of three statuses: the fit completed, it raised, or it finished without sealing a record. A failure to write the evidence stops the batch, because the outcomes of the remaining entries could not be recorded.

docs.title: The evidence store
docs.text:
Records are written atomically and never overwritten, and the index is rewritten after every outcome, so an interrupted batch keeps everything that finished. The directory must be fresh, since a store is never appended to.

Reopening a store re-verifies it. The plan hash is recomputed from the persisted plan, every record is verified against its own hash and against the plan slot it claims, records under one dataset name must share one data fingerprint, and a file in the records directory that the index does not list raises an error. The reopened store is read-only. Each store also records the environment it ran in: the KD, Python and torch versions, the platform string, and the commit if the run happened inside a checkout.

docs.title: Consensus across runs
docs.text:
build_consensus is a pure function over a sealed store. Runs are grouped by the canonical set of terms they selected, so two runs that print different strings but selected the same law are placed in the same class:

from kd.harness import EvidenceStore, build_consensus

store = EvidenceStore.load("out/burgers-seeds")
report = build_consensus(store)
for dataset_consensus in report.datasets:
    for cls in dataset_consensus.classes:
        members = ", ".join(f"{m.instrument}/seed{m.seed}" for m in cls.members)
        print(cls.structure_key[:10], "|", members)
        print("   ", cls.terms)
    for pair in dataset_consensus.adjacency:
        print("adjacency", pair.structure_key_a[:10], pair.structure_key_b[:10],
              pair.relation, round(pair.jaccard, 2))

ed0de3fa1f | sga/seed0, sga/seed1
    ('diff_x(u_x)', 'mul(u,u_x)', 'u_t')
2b7f162ff3 | sga/seed2
    ('diff2_x(sub(u,x))', 'diff_x(n2(u))', 'u_t')
adjacency ed0de3fa1f 2b7f162ff3 disjoint 0.0

The three runs produced two classes. The second class is the same law in a different notation: diff_x(n2(u)) is the derivative of u², which equals 2·u·u_x, and diff2_x(sub(u, x)) is the second derivative of u - x, which equals u_xx. Seed 2 therefore selected the same law written differently. Term sets are grouped rather than simplified, and the adjacency line compares them literally, leaving out the shared left-hand side u_t, so it reports the two classes as disjoint: it does not detect that two spellings evaluate to the same column. To check whether a split is a difference of notation, fit both term sets on the data with kd.evaluate_terms and compare the recovered laws.

Each class is described along four independent axes: whether the structure agrees, whether the support agrees, whether the coefficients agree, and whether the empirical fit agrees. The four are reported separately, without a combined confidence number, because they can disagree with one another. The report also records how far the corroboration extends, from several algorithms across different derivative sources down to a single run, so a class supported by three seeds of one algorithm is not read as a class supported by three algorithms.

The report renders to Markdown and to a JSON artifact. Both are deterministic: the same evidence renders byte for byte the same way.

docs.title: Equation representation
docs.text:
KD uses function-call term strings to exchange equation structure between algorithms and platform services. Each algorithm holds candidates in its own data structure internally and converts them on the way out. Algorithm term libraries and kd.evaluate_terms use this notation, with different requirements for accepted terms.

The notation describes structure rather than display. It is not intended to resemble the notation used in a paper. It separates equation structure from the way an algorithm displays its answer.

Public results use shared equation and result objects. A plugin's checkpoint state is an exception: it keeps the native representation needed by that same plugin to restore its search.

docs.title: Term syntax
docs.text:
A term is a prefix function call, or a terminal token.

Written Meaning u the field itself u_x, u_xx first and second spatial derivatives, as terminal tokens diff_x(u), diff2_x(u) the same derivatives, as calls diff_x(diff2_x(u)) third derivative mul(u, u_x) u times u_x add(u_xx, mul(u, u_x)) a sum of two terms

The built-in operators are add, sub, mul, div, neg, n2 (square), n3 (cube), recip (reciprocal), sin, cos, exp, log, and lap, the spatial Laplacian: it sums the second derivative over the dataset's spatial axes, so on two spatial axes lap(u) is u_xx + u_yy, and lap(lap(u)) gives the biharmonic term. Six of them route through guarded implementations: div and recip floor a near-zero denominator, log floors a near-zero argument, and exp, n2 and n3 clamp their input magnitude, so none of these six produces an inf or a nan from a zero denominator or an overflowing exponent.

Coefficients are not part of a term. An algorithm returns terms, coefficients and a left-hand side separately, and the term string describes structure only. Two terms are therefore identical regardless of the coefficient fitted for them: mul(u, u_x) has the same term string whether the fit returned -1 or -0.5. Canonical term libraries, including those used by PySINDy and PySR for PDE data, require terms without numeric literals: write u rather than mul(2, u) and let the fit determine its coefficient.

The evaluation entry points kd.validate_terms and kd.evaluate_terms also accept numeric literals such as mul(2, u). A nonzero factor multiplying a whole term can be absorbed into its fitted coefficient. Acceptance by these entry points does not imply acceptance by an algorithm's canonical term library.

max_order sets the highest derivative order available as a terminal token. It is a parameter of kd.evaluate_terms and kd.validate_terms and defaults to 2, so u_xx can be written directly. Derivatives written as calls are not bounded by max_order, so diff_x(diff2_x(u)) resolves under the default settings, because the on-the-fly finite-difference scheme reaches third order.

docs.title: Notation on the input side
docs.text:
Candidate-term libraries and operator sets are written in the same IR as the terms that come back out:

kd.PySINDyConfig().terms          # ('u', 'u_x', 'u_xx', 'mul(u, u_x)')
kd.PySRConfig().terms             # ('u', 'u_x', 'u_xx', 'mul(u, u_x)')
kd.DLGAConfig().library           # ['u', 'u_x', 'u_xx', 'u_xxx']
kd.DiscoverConfig().library.operators
# ['add', 'mul', 'sub', 'div', 'sin', 'cos', 'diff_x', 'diff2_x']

A candidate library can be reused where its terms meet the receiving algorithm's requirements for operators, derivatives and data. kd.evaluate_terms can refit the terms under its own validation contract. When a library carries a terminal token above the default max_order (u_xxx in the DLGAConfig list above), raise max_order to that order for the refit:

kd.evaluate_terms(dataset, kd.DLGAConfig().library, max_order=3)

docs.title: Conversion per algorithm
docs.text:
• SGA-PDE searches expression trees and maps the node names on the way out: + becomes add, * becomes mul, ^2 becomes n2, and the two derivative operators d and d^2 render as diff_x(...) / diff2_x(...) against the differentiation axis.
  • PySR returns a SymPy expression. It is expanded, split at the top-level sum, and each part is stripped of its numeric coefficient and serialized to IR; the platform refits the coefficients.
  • DISCOVER builds its trees from the IR operator names directly; the operator set above is its own.
  • PySINDy and DLGA-PDE select columns from a candidate library that is already IR.

docs.title: The equation in a result
docs.text:
model.best_expr_ is a display string and each algorithm renders it its own way (SGA-PDE bakes the fitted coefficients into the text), so it is not the thing to align two algorithms on.

The equation-level object is model.result_.equation: terms paired with their coefficients, plus a left-hand side LhsSpec(field='u', axis='t', order=1), that is, u_t.

docs.title: Structural comparison
docs.text:
kd.law_signature(equation) reduces an equation to a signature: the left-hand side joins the term set, terms are sorted in canonical form, and the coefficient vector is normalized with a fixed sign anchor. Two equations with the same structure get the same structure_key, whatever string each of them prints.

For example, the catalog sums add(diff_x(diff2_x(u)), mul(u,u_x)) and add(mul(u,u_x), diff_x(diff2_x(u))) differ in order. A comparison uses the terms and equation structure rather than that display order.

Canonical form reorders the arguments of add and mul (they commute) and performs no algebraic simplification, so mul(u, u_x) and mul(u_x, u) are one term. Stopping at commutativity is deliberate: simplification means a body of algebraic rules, and the more rules there are, the less obvious the reason two equations were called the same one.

The two runs below differ only in how the PySINDy candidate library is spelled and ordered:

import kd

dataset = kd.load_kdv()
for terms in [
    ("u_x", "u_xx", "diff_x(diff2_x(u))", "mul(u, u_x)"),
    ("mul(u_x, u)", "diff_x(diff2_x(u))", "u_x", "u_xx"),
]:
    model = kd.Model(
        algorithm="pysindy",
        config=kd.PySINDyConfig(terms=terms, threshold=1e-3, seed=42),
        verbose=False,
    )
    model.fit(dataset)
    signature = kd.law_signature(model.result_.equation)
    print(model.best_expr_)
    print(signature.structure_key, signature.terms)

add(diff_x(diff2_x(u)), mul(u,u_x))
1f62a06976f85133 ('diff_x(diff2_x(u))', 'mul(u,u_x)', 'u_t')
add(mul(u,u_x), diff_x(diff2_x(u)))
1f62a06976f85133 ('diff_x(diff2_x(u))', 'mul(u,u_x)', 'u_t')

The display strings differ while the structure_key is the same. That key is used to align results across algorithms.

Settle on one spelling for the derivatives before you align on it. The canonical form does no algebraic rewriting, so the terminal token u_xx and the call diff2_x(u) are two different terms, and one equation written both ways yields two different structure_key values. Give the algorithms you are comparing libraries in the same spelling: either both u_xxx or both diff_x(diff2_x(u)).

docs.title: Platform and plugins
docs.text: KD is organized as a platform with algorithm plugins. Each plugin implements the algorithm-specific search procedure and scientific logic, while the platform provides the infrastructure shared across algorithms, including data preparation, derivative computation, term evaluation, coefficient fitting, run management, visualization, checkpointing, and batch execution.

docs.title: The plugin contract
docs.text:
An algorithm plugin implements the following members. It prepares itself against the components the platform hands it, proposes candidates, evaluates them, updates itself on the results, exposes its best score and best expression, serializes its configuration and its state, and builds its own final result together with the target that result is expressed in.

KD checks these members when a run starts. A missing member raises a single error that names every gap, so an incomplete algorithm fails before the search begins.

The platform provides the iteration loop, keeps batches in 1:1 correspondence with the candidates the algorithm proposed, calls back for early stopping and for figure data, writes checkpoints atomically from the algorithm's own state, keeps the run record, and assembles the result object.

The platform does not re-score the winning candidate. The algorithm builds its own final result because the residuals and the target must be computed in the same domain. If the platform computed the residuals while the algorithm supplied the target, the two could refer to different quantities.

docs.title: Optional services
docs.text:
The platform also provides derivatives, term execution, the design matrix, the linear solver, and surrogate network training. An algorithm uses the services that fit its method and implements the rest itself. The table below lists what each algorithm implements on its own.

PDEDataset stores observations, axes and the field-axis-order specification of the left-hand side. Derivatives are computed on demand. They may depend on a surrogate training run performed after dataset construction, so the dataset does not store them. The evaluation services execute term strings into columns, assemble the design matrix, solve least-squares problems and compute MSE, NMSE, R² and AIC. The executor's protected operators guard small denominators and large arguments as described in term syntax.

Algorithm What it brings of its own SGA-PDE expression-tree search, its own sparse fit, and its own surrogate when run in autograd mode DLGA-PDE genetic search over a term genome and its own evaluators; the platform trains its surrogate network from the configured values DISCOVER a policy network over token sequences; candidates are scored through the platform evaluator EqGPT a pretrained transformer; two of its three modes run without platform derivatives at all, on evaluators it builds per case LLM4ED a language model proposing candidates, with the finite-difference templates and the sparse fit ported alongside it PySR an external search engine; the platform supplies the design matrix and refits the coefficients PySINDy an external engine whose native coefficients are kept, with the platform refit recorded next to them as a cross-check

The services used depend on the mode as well as the algorithm. SGA-PDE and LLM4ED include their own candidate evaluation and sparse-fitting paths; EqGPT's multi-case wave and steady modes build their own evaluations without platform derivatives. Derivative sources lists the provider declared by every mode.

docs.title: Declared capabilities
docs.text:
Each algorithm declares its capabilities as data on the class. The declaration covers the equation forms and data layouts of each mode, the source of that mode's derivatives, the name and direction of its score, whether the algorithm returns its answer in one shot, which parameters exist and which of them survive a resume, which parameters change the scientific identity of a run, and how far each mode can honour a sketch.

kd.instrument_schemas() returns those declarations, one entry per algorithm:

schema = next(s for s in kd.instrument_schemas() if s["algorithm"] == "pysindy")
print(schema["score_kind"], schema["score_direction"], schema["one_shot"])
print(schema["modes"])
print([(knob["name"], knob["resume_tier"]) for knob in schema["knobs"]])

NMSE min True
[{'name': 'default', 'forms': ['EVOLUTION'], 'topologies': ['grid'], 'provider_kind': 'finite_diff', 'description': '', 'sketch': {'fixed_terms': 'lowered', 'anchors': 'fit_enforced', 'hole_count': 'exit_checked', 'derivative_order': 'generation_enforced', 'operator_set': 'generation_enforced', 'field_axis_set': 'generation_enforced'}}]
[('threshold', 'init_only'), ('max_iter', 'init_only'), ('normalize_columns', 'init_only')]

The sketch block of a mode is that mode's answer, clause by clause, for a partially specified equation passed to Model.fit(sketch=...): lowered, generation_enforced, fit_enforced, exit_checked, or unsupported. All six clauses are always listed, so a mode that supports none of them still carries six keys.

The platform reads the declaration rather than keeping its own tables of the same information. It uses the declaration to decide which derivative provider to build, which datasets to accept, how to label a score, and what a resume may change. Programs driving KD read the same call, and the specification strips and parameter tables on this site are generated from it, so they cannot diverge from the code they describe.

The cost class in that entry (light, medium, heavy) is declared by the algorithm rather than measured at runtime. It is an estimate used for routing.

Algorithms are registered inside the package, and the seven listed above are the ones a released version provides. An additional algorithm is added to KD together with its declaration.

docs.title: Parameter tiers and resuming
docs.text:
Whether a run can be resumed depends on which parameters changed between the checkpoint and the new kd.Model.

The parameter table on every algorithm page has a "Resume" column, and every parameter carries a badge there: resume-safe or init-only. The algorithm declares that badge itself, and the badge determines whether a new value takes effect on a resume.

Tier Meaning resume-safe the new value takes effect when resuming from a checkpoint, and the stored search state stays valid init-only the new value applies to a fresh fit only; resuming with the change raises

A third tier is not shown in the tables. Fields that change the scientific identity of the run, such as the candidate library and derivative semantics, are identity-breaking: changing one makes the two segments a different experiment, and the resume raises.

Any config field with no declared tier is treated as init-only. The default refuses because the two mistakes have different consequences. A field that should have been declared resume-safe requires one line of edit to correct, while a resume that succeeded across two different configurations leaves the error in the result.

The tables use the config field names. Two fields are spelled differently as kd.Model keywords: num is population, and use_autograd is derivatives.

docs.title: Checkpoint writing
docs.text:
Setting checkpoint_dir to a directory enables checkpointing. checkpoint_every sets the interval in iterations, and a checkpoint_final.pt is written when the run ends. The directory is managed by a manifest.json and cannot be reused: pointing at a non-empty directory raises, so each run needs a fresh directory. checkpoint_keep_last bounds how many periodic checkpoints are retained, and the final one is neither counted nor pruned.

import kd

dataset = kd.load_kdv()
model = kd.Model(
    algorithm="sga", generations=4, seed=42, verbose=False,
    checkpoint_dir="out/kdv-ckpt", checkpoint_every=2,
)
model.fit(dataset)

docs.title: The manifest
docs.text:
kd.load_checkpoint_manifest returns the directory's entries in write order. It is read-only and performs no repair or cleanup. kd.resolve_checkpoint selects the resume point from these entries (the latest periodic checkpoint or completed final; a final stamped crashed is never selected) rather than globbing the directory:

point = kd.resolve_checkpoint("out/kdv-ckpt")          # or iteration=2 for a rollback
print(point.path, point.iteration)

for entry in kd.load_checkpoint_manifest("out/kdv-ckpt"):
    print(entry.filename, entry.kind, entry.final_status, entry.iteration, entry.best_score)

checkpoint_000000.pt periodic None 0 -18.37657775848694
checkpoint_000002.pt periodic None 2 -18.37657775848694
checkpoint_final.pt final completed 3 -18.37657775848694

An entry also carries best_expression, algorithm, seed, created_at, kd_version and more. kind separates periodic from final checkpoints, and final_status is set on the final one only: completed for a run that finished, crashed for the final checkpoint a crashed run left behind, so the two are distinguishable. Both values have exported constants, kd.KIND_FINAL and kd.FINAL_STATUS_COMPLETED.

docs.title: Resume a run
docs.text:
fit takes a checkpoint path as resume_from. A resume restores the search state: the population, the controller weights, and the current best. The number of generations comes from this kd.Model, and the parameters are judged by the tiers above. seed is not in the tier table, so it takes the unregistered-field default of init-only. A plain resume keeps the seed the checkpoint was written with, and a different seed is rejected. Passing reseed=True to fit turns the resume into a branch: it keeps the restored search state and re-derives the random streams from this model's seed, so a changed seed is accepted. Branching is available for the algorithms whose segmentation.reseed declaration is true, today every algorithm except pysindy, whose one-pass fit archives a conclusion rather than search progress.

resumed = kd.Model(algorithm="sga", generations=8, seed=42, verbose=False, population=25)
resumed.fit(dataset, resume_from="out/kdv-ckpt/checkpoint_final.pt")
print(resumed.result_.equation)

u_t = -u*u_x - 0.0025*u_x_xx

population is resume-safe, so the resume accepts the new value. With a changed seed, which takes the init-only default:

changed = kd.Model(algorithm="sga", generations=8, seed=7, verbose=False)
changed.fit(dataset, resume_from="out/kdv-ckpt/checkpoint_final.pt")

ValueError: resume config mismatch for algorithm 'sga': init_only field(s) changed
vs the checkpoint: seed (stored 42 -> live 7). These fields can only be set on a
fresh fit; drop resume_from or revert them.

Passing reseed=True turns that same change into a branch:

branched = kd.Model(algorithm="sga", generations=8, seed=7, verbose=False)
branched.fit(dataset, resume_from="out/kdv-ckpt/checkpoint_final.pt", reseed=True)
print(branched.result_.equation)

u_t = -u*u_x - 0.0025*u_x_xx

And with an identity-breaking change, the derivative source (derivatives="autograd", the config field use_autograd):

ValueError: resume config mismatch for algorithm 'sga': identity_breaking field(s)
changed vs the checkpoint: use_autograd (stored False -> live True). A science-identity
change starts a new lineage: run a fresh fit in a new checkpoint directory; this
checkpoint cannot be resumed under the new config.

Every message names the field and both of its values.

docs.title: Add generations
docs.text: generations is not a config field. For the iterative algorithms it maps to the iteration budget, so extending a run means raising generations on the resuming model. PySR stores its populations and hall of fame in the checkpoint, so raising generations on a resume extends that segment's PySR search. PySINDy solves in one pass, so for it generations cannot be raised on a resume.

docs.title: The two manifests
docs.text: The manifest.json above belongs to a checkpoint directory and lists what is in it. A finished run carries a second, unrelated manifest at model.result_.manifest. It records the facts needed to reproduce that run and excludes anything that varies between two identical runs: the dataset fingerprint, the KD version, the seed, the term library for the algorithms that take one, and, when the run continued an earlier one, where it resumed from.

docs.title: Score conventions and comparability
docs.text:
KD does not rank algorithms against one another. It provides a way to refit candidate terms against the same data so that the resulting numbers can be compared.

model.best_score_ is that algorithm's own objective value. Its name and its direction are declared per algorithm: some report AIC, some report NMSE, and some report a reward they define themselves, with both min and max directions in use. The score cell in the spec strip at the top of each algorithm page reports these two facts. Equal score values from two different algorithms therefore do not indicate equal quality.

model.result_.score_kind and score_direction expose those two facts programmatically. score_kind is a stable identifier. Two scores are comparable only when the kind, the dataset and the scorer all match, and across algorithms these conditions generally do not hold.

For example, SGA-PDE's AIC and DISCOVER's reward are different quantities with different directions. KD does not convert them into one score or rewrite best_score_; an independent refit supplies a separate comparison measurement.

docs.title: Refit against the same data
docs.text:
kd.evaluate_terms takes a set of terms back to the same data and fits them once, using the same derivatives and the same least-squares solver. This requires one additional step compared with converting the native scores, and it produces a number that refers to a specific fit rather than to a conversion. When the term sets under comparison are all evaluated this way, the resulting nmse, r2 and coefficients are measured in the same frame.

import kd

dataset = kd.load_kdv()
for terms in [
    ["mul(u, u_x)", "diff2_x(u)"],
    ["mul(u, u_x)", "diff_x(diff2_x(u))"],
]:
    result = kd.evaluate_terms(dataset, terms)
    print(terms)
    print("  nmse", format(result.nmse, ".3e"),
          "coefficients", [round(float(c), 4) for c in result.coefficients])

['mul(u, u_x)', 'diff2_x(u)']
  nmse 8.489e-01 coefficients [-0.0902, -0.0024]
['mul(u, u_x)', 'diff_x(diff2_x(u))']
  nmse 2.903e-05 coefficients [-1.0, -0.0025]

The two sets differ in a second versus a third derivative. The second set is the true support of KdV: the refit returns -1.0 and -0.0025, matching the reference equation, at an nmse more than four orders of magnitude lower. These two nmse values can be compared with each other, because both fits used the same data, the same derivatives and the same solver.

Besides nmse, mse, r2 and coefficients, the returned EvaluationResult carries condition_number, the condition number of the columns this fit was handed, which indicates whether the candidate terms are collinear.

docs.title: The comparison figure
docs.text:
kd.VizEngine.render_comparison overlays several runs: their score curves, a bar chart of final scores and R², and a summary table carrying each run's expression, nmse, r2 and how its term set differs from the first run's.

The mean and standard deviation band over those curves is drawn only across runs that share one algorithm and one declared score kind and direction. If a run reporting AIC is overlaid with one reporting a reward, the band is dropped, a subtitle on the figure states that the curve trends are not comparable, and the accompanying warning points to the final nmse and r2 instead. Two different algorithms that report the same metric also lose the band, because a single band over two populations does not describe either of them.

docs.title: Accepted term forms
docs.text:
Each string is a single term in function-call form (see Equation representation). Infix notation and a top-level sum are rejected, and the rejection carries the reason. kd.validate_terms classifies terms without fitting them, so it can be used as a first pass:

report = kd.validate_terms(dataset, ["u + u_xx", "add(u, u_xx)", "mul(u, u_x)"])
print(report.valid)
for rejection in report.rejected:
    print(rejection.term, "|", rejection.reason)

['mul(u, u_x)']
u + u_xx | syntax: non-canonical term (funcall IR required); Infix operators (e.g., 'a + b') are not allowed. Use function-call IR: add(a, b), mul(a, b), etc.
add(u, u_xx) | composite: top-level additive structure; submit as 2 separate terms: ['u', 'u_xx']

kd.evaluate_terms is strict by default. One rejected term raises InvalidTermsError carrying the complete list of rejections rather than only the first one. Pass skip_invalid=True and the rejected terms are dropped, the remaining terms are fitted, and one warning names what was dropped.

Terminology

model.result_.run_record.evidence.headline_coefficient_source records who performed the fit (native for coefficients the algorithm produced itself, platform_refit for coefficients the platform refitted). It qualifies coefficients, mse, nmse and r2 only, not the score. Score semantics are governed by score_kind.

docs.title: Getting started: discover a PDE from field data
docs.text:
KD recovers the Burgers equation from a bundled benchmark dataset whose equation is known. This notebook loads the data, inspects the field, fits a symbolic model in one call, compares the result with the known equation, and plots the convergence curve.

import kd

ds = kd.load_burgers()
print(ds.ground_truth)

u_t = -u * u_x + 0.1 * u_xx

docs.title: Look at the data
docs.text:
The dataset contains a field u sampled on an (x, t) grid. Before fitting, kd.preview prints the grid, the field, and the left-hand-side derivative that KD will use.

kd.preview(ds)
kd.viz.plots.plot_field(ds)

Dataset: burgers
Axes:
     x | n=256  | range [-8.000, 7.938] | step 0.0625 (uniform)
     t | n=201  | range [0.000, 10.000] | step 0.05 (uniform)
Fields:
     u | dtype=float64 | shape=(256, 201) | min=-1.000 max=1.000 mean=0.000 (NaN=0)
LHS: u_t  (field='u', axis='t')
Status: ready to fit

docs.title: Fit a model
docs.text:
SGA-PDE searches over symbolic expression trees and scores candidate right-hand sides against the target derivative. generations sets the search budget. The value below is small enough to run quickly and large enough to recover a Burgers-like equation.

model = kd.Model(algorithm="sga", generations=5, seed=0, verbose=False).fit(ds)
print(model.result_.equation)
print(model.best_score_)

u_t = -u*u_x + 0.1002*u_xx
-28.776748939600004

docs.title: Compare to ground truth
docs.text:
The discovered equation is KD's best symbolic right-hand side for u_t. The exact string can differ from the compact textbook form, so the check is whether it contains the nonlinear advection and diffusion terms.

print(f"Discovered  : {model.result_.equation}")
print(f"Ground truth: {ds.ground_truth}")

Discovered  : u_t = -u*u_x + 0.1002*u_xx
Ground truth: u_t = -u * u_x + 0.1 * u_xx

docs.title: Visualize
docs.text:
plot_convergence draws the recorded best-score curve, labels it with the algorithm's score kind (AIC for SGA), and notes when the best score was reached on the first iteration. It creates its own figure; the returned list contains any plot notes.

from kd.viz.plots import plot_convergence

plot_convergence(model.result_);

docs.title: The report
docs.text:
model.report writes every supported figure and an HTML report, and displays the report here. The same files remain in the output directory.

model.report("../out/getting_started")

Report: ../out/getting_started/report.html

docs.title: KdV walkthrough: from a field to its equation
docs.text:
KD recovers the Korteweg-de Vries equation, u_t = -u u_x - 0.0025 u_xxx, from a bundled benchmark field whose equation is known. The search is SGA-PDE at the budget its recovery suite validates (200 generations, population 20, seed 42). Four calls carry the whole walkthrough: load the data, draw it, fit, render the report. Every output below is committed from one execution, so the numbers are what the code printed.

import kd

docs.title: The data
docs.text:
The KdV field ships with KD as a 256 by 201 grid in x and t, taken from the SGA-PDE benchmark set. kd.preview audits the grid spacing, the field values and the left-hand side before any search runs; plot_field draws the field as it was measured.

dataset = kd.load_kdv()
kd.preview(dataset)

Dataset: kdv
Axes:
     x | n=256  | range [-1.000, 0.992] | step 0.007812 (uniform)
     t | n=201  | range [0.000, 1.000] | step 0.005 (uniform)
Fields:
     u | dtype=float64 | shape=(256, 201) | min=-1.000 max=2.309 mean=0.000 (NaN=0)
LHS: u_t  (field='u', axis='t')
Status: ready to fit

kd.viz.plots.plot_field(dataset)

docs.title: Fit SGA-PDE
docs.text:
generations=200 and seed=42 are the settings the KdV recovery suite pins; population, tree depth and the sparse-regression sweep stay at the SGAConfig defaults. The third-derivative coefficient is 400 times smaller than the advection coefficient, which is what the coarse sweep has to keep. The fit took about 2 minutes in this run.

model = kd.Model(algorithm="sga", generations=200, seed=42, verbose=False).fit(dataset)
model

Model(algorithm='sga', fitted=True, best_expr='u_t = -0.0025*u_x_xx - 0.5*(u**2)_x', best_score=-19.59)

docs.title: Recovered law and the reference
docs.text:
SGA-PDE writes the advection term as -0.5 * diff_x(n2(u)), with n2 KD's protected square; by the chain rule this is -u u_x. It writes u_xxx as the nested diff2_x(u_x). In this run the fitted coefficients are -0.500004 for the advection term (reference -0.5, relative error 9.0e-6) and -0.002500 for the dispersion term (reference -0.0025, relative error 5.0e-5); the search selected no other term.

print(f"Discovered : {model.result_.equation}")
print(f"Reference  : {dataset.ground_truth}")

Discovered : u_t = -0.0025*u_x_xx - 0.5*(u**2)_x
Reference  : u_t = -u * u_x - 0.0025 * u_xxx

docs.title: The report
docs.text:
model.report renders every figure this fit supports and one HTML page that embeds them: the convergence curve, the presence of each term and the spread of scores among the best recorded structures, the parity plot, the equation and its tree, the coefficient bars, the residual histogram and heatmap, the measured field next to the field integrated from the discovered equation, the time slices, the error heatmap, the PDE residual field, and SGA-PDE's own search diagnostics. The page is shown below; the same files are written to the output directory.

model.report("../out/kdv_walkthrough")

Report: ../out/kdv_walkthrough/report.html

docs.title: Noisy Burgers walkthrough: a field with 15% noise, and its equation
docs.text:
KD recovers the Burgers equation, u_t = -u u_x + 0.1 u_xx, from the bundled benchmark field after 15% relative Gaussian noise is added to every sample. The search is DLGA, which first fits a neural network to the noisy field and takes every derivative from that network instead of from the samples; Xu et al. (2020) report Burgers recovered at this noise level, and KD's recovery suite pins the same case. Four calls carry the walkthrough: load and noise the data, draw it, fit, render the report. Every output below is committed from one execution.

import kd

docs.title: The data
docs.text:
kd.load_burgers ships the 256 by 201 Burgers field of the SGA-PDE benchmark set. kd.add_noise returns a copy with Gaussian noise whose standard deviation is 15% of the field's own; the seed fixes the draw, and noise_level on the result records what was added. kd.preview audits the grid and the field, plot_field draws it as it would be measured.

dataset = kd.add_noise(kd.load_burgers(), 0.15, seed=2026)
kd.preview(dataset)

Dataset: burgers
Axes:
     x | n=256  | range [-8.000, 7.938] | step 0.0625 (uniform)
     t | n=201  | range [0.000, 10.000] | step 0.05 (uniform)
Fields:
     u | dtype=float64 | shape=(256, 201) | min=-1.226 max=1.288 mean=0.000 (NaN=0)
LHS: u_t  (field='u', axis='t')
Status: ready to fit

kd.viz.plots.plot_field(dataset)

docs.title: Differentiate the samples directly
docs.text:
Finite differences of a noisy field amplify the noise: at this level the derivative columns carry little of the signal, and a search over them keeps whatever fits the noise. SGA-PDE at the budget its Burgers recovery suite validates on the clean field (100 generations, seed 42) returns u_t = 0.002134 u^2 x^3 here, a term with no derivative in it, after about 3 minutes.

direct = kd.Model(algorithm="sga", generations=100, seed=42, verbose=False).fit(dataset)
print(f"Discovered : {direct.result_.equation}")
print(f"Reference  : {dataset.ground_truth}")

Discovered : u_t = 0.002134*u**2*x**3
Reference  : u_t = -u * u_x + 0.1 * u_xx

docs.title: Fit DLGA
docs.text:
DLGA fits a neural network to the noisy samples and takes every derivative, u_t included, from that network. DLGAConfig.burgers_preset locks the length penalty validated for Burgers; surrogate_max_epochs=50_000 is the network's training budget, and pop_size=50 with generations=20 is the genetic search budget the recovery suite runs at. The fit took about 158 minutes in this run.

model = kd.Model(
    algorithm="dlga",
    generations=20,
    config=kd.DLGAConfig.burgers_preset(pop_size=50, seed=0, surrogate_max_epochs=50_000),
    verbose=False,
).fit(dataset)
model

DLGA recovered expression has nmse=0.0258 and length=8 tokens. The default epsilon=1e-03 was tuned for raw-MSE-era fitness magnitudes; under the NMSE-era selector the length penalty contribution is smaller, so the GA may include small-coefficient noise terms. Truth structure is still recovered (see is_recovery_success superset match). To get a cleaner surface expression, raise DLGAConfig.epsilon to ~1e-2 to 5e-2 — see DLGAPlugin docstring for per-PDE recommendations.





Model(algorithm='dlga', fitted=True, best_expr='u_t = -0.9829*u*u_x - 0.002841*u*u_xxx + 1.184e-6*u_x*u_xxx**2 + 0.1039*u_xx', best_score=0.03381)

docs.title: Recovered law and the reference
docs.text:
DLGA prints the structure it selected; the fitted coefficients are on the equation panel of the report below. In this run they are -0.9829 for u u_x (reference -1, relative error 1.7%) and 0.1039 for u_xx (reference 0.1, relative error 3.9%). Two further terms stayed in the expression with coefficients far below those two, -0.002841 u u_xxx and 1.184e-6 u_x u_xxx^2; the fit's NMSE is 0.0258. The warning printed by the fit says the same thing about them: at epsilon=1e-3 the length penalty leaves such small-coefficient terms in, and a larger epsilon shortens the expression.

print(f"Discovered : {model.result_.equation}")
print(f"Reference  : {dataset.ground_truth}")

Discovered : u_t = -0.9829*u*u_x - 0.002841*u*u_xxx + 1.184e-6*u_x*u_xxx**2 + 0.1039*u_xx
Reference  : u_t = -u * u_x + 0.1 * u_xx

docs.title: The report
docs.text:
model.report renders every figure this fit supports and one HTML page that embeds them: the convergence curve, the parity plot, the equation and its tree, the coefficient bars, the residual figures, the noisy field next to the field integrated from the discovered equation, the time slices, the error heatmap, the PDE residual field, and DLGA's own diagnostics, including the training curve of the network that supplied the derivatives. The page is shown below; the same files are written to the output directory.

model.report("../out/noisy_burgers_walkthrough")

Report: ../out/noisy_burgers_walkthrough/report.html
