docs.title: Column chromatography
docs.text: This page fits two algorithms, DISCOVER and PySR, to the same dataset and compares the expressions they return. Both are called through kd.Model, so the two runs differ in the algorithm name and in the search parameters specific to each algorithm.

docs.title: The dataset
docs.text:
kd.load_tlc_cc() returns 74 rows from an automated column chromatography platform. Each row is one experimental condition: the two feature columns are the thin-layer retardation factor R_F and the petroleum-ether fraction r of the eluent, and the target is the retention volume V_S in millilitres, averaged over the compounds run at that condition. Xu et al. (2025) published a formula relating the three:

\[V_S = \dfrac{r}{0.147\,R_F + 0.0114}\]

docs.title: Run both algorithms
docs.text:
import kd

table = kd.load_tlc_cc()

discover = kd.Model(
    algorithm="discover", generations=200, seed=0,
    batch_size=1000, max_length=15, reward_alpha=0.005,
).fit(table)

pysr = kd.Model(
    algorithm="pysr", generations=100, seed=0,
    maxsize=10, binary_operators=("+", "*", "/"), unary_operators=(),
).fit(table)

Neither call specifies candidate terms. DISCOVER searches over the table's own column names together with the operators add, sub, mul and div. PySR receives the same two columns and the operators +, * and /. Both return a REGRESSION equation on result_.equation and the nondominated set of the search on result_.pareto_front().

Pareto front of each algorithm, plotted on a common accuracy axis: R² over all 74 rows against the size of the expression. The two size axes are not the same measure, since PySR counts nodes and DISCOVER counts tokens. The dashed line marks the fit of the published formula on these rows, 0.876. Circles mark the front entry equal to that formula, and diamonds mark the answer each run selected.

docs.title: The published formula on both fronts
docs.text:
Each algorithm returns an expression together with an outer coefficient fitted for it. Dividing through puts both in the form of the published formula:

a b R² Published 0.147 0.0114 0.876 DISCOVER, 5 tokens 0.1507 0.01110 0.876 PySR, 7 nodes 0.1496 0.01121 0.876

The two coefficient pairs are within 2.6% of the published values and within 1% of each other, from one run of each algorithm at a fixed seed.

docs.title: The selected answers
docs.text: Neither run selects the published formula. Three of the 74 rows were measured at r = 0, where that formula predicts zero against measured volumes of 4.41, 5.17 and 5.86 mL, so an expression carrying an intercept fits the table more closely, and a shorter expression that omits r is cheaper under both complexity measures. DISCOVER selected a nine-token expression with an R² of 0.898, and PySR selected the five-node expression 5.892 / (R_F + 0.0669) with an R² of 0.864. The published formula appears between these on both fronts.

docs.title: Breaking waves
docs.text:
EqGPT discovered a law for breaking-wave surface elevation from 12 wave-tank experiments (Xu et al., Nat Commun 16, 10255, 2025). KD hosts EqGPT as a search plugin and reproduces that published result, with permission of the authors, on the same scattered (t, x, eta) measurements:

\[\eta_t + c_1\,\eta_x + c_2\,\eta_{xxx} + c_3\,(\eta\,\eta_x)_{xx} = 0\]

In KD's notation the surface elevation is the field u, so the recovered right-hand side is the term set {u_x, u_xxx, diff2_x(mul(u, u_x))} with per-experiment coefficients.

import kd
from kd.core.expr import to_sympy
from kd.data.loaders import load_wave_breaking_datasets

docs.title: Optional data preview
docs.text:
WaveBreaking.pkl holds surface-elevation records from the BUBER and EURUS campaigns in the 27.2 m glass-walled wave tank at Imperial College London, where the air-water interface was reconstructed frame by frame from three cameras running at 20 Hz; the paper's discovery uses the 12 "N" experiments. Each case is a scattered point cloud (t, x, eta) with no grid, so the dataset is SCATTERED topology. EqGPT fits all 12 cases; the preview below shows the first N case in sorted order. kd.preview describes its axes and field, and kd.viz.plots.plot_field draws the observed surface elevation. These preview calls are optional and do not affect the fit. The later report describes the fitted equation and its diagnostics.

cases = load_wave_breaking_datasets(case_filter="N")
primary_name = next(iter(cases))
primary_ds = cases[primary_name]

print(f"N cases ({len(cases)}): {', '.join(cases)}")
kd.preview(primary_ds)
kd.viz.plots.plot_field(primary_ds)

N cases (12): N_G2Tp12A080_broad, N_G2Tp12A090_broad, N_G2Tp12A100_broad, N_G2Tp12A105_broad, N_G2Tp13A090_broad, N_G2Tp13A096_broad, N_G2Tp13A105_broad, N_G2Tp13A130_broad, N_G3Tp12A083_broad, N_G3Tp12A095_broad, N_G3Tp12A100_broad, N_G3Tp12A117_broad
Dataset: wave-breaking-N_G2Tp12A080_broad
Axes:
     t | n=507868 | range [0.050, 5.250] | step n/a (scattered)
     x | n=507868 | range [8.148, 12.548] | step n/a (scattered)
Fields:
     u | dtype=float64 | shape=(507868,) | min=-0.071 max=0.109 mean=-0.000 (NaN=0)
LHS: u_t  (field='u', axis='t')
Status: ready to fit

docs.title: Multi-case fit
docs.text:
EqGPTConfig.wave_preset pins the paper's setup: multi-case wave mode (case_filter="N"), sparsity_alpha=0.02. Per generation the pretrained GPT proposes candidate right-hand sides; KD scores each candidate on every experiment (per-case surrogate and least-squares fit) and keeps the candidate with the best mean reward over the cases that scored successfully. seed=21 makes the run reproduce the same result each time, through KD's CPU torch RNG stream.

The cell below runs a 5-generation search across all 12 experiments, loading the per-case surrogates and the measurement records.

DEMO_SEED = 21

model = kd.Model(
    algorithm="eqgpt",
    generations=5,
    config=kd.EqGPTConfig.wave_preset(seed=DEMO_SEED, primary_case=primary_name),
).fit(primary_ds)

print(f"Reproduced structure : {to_sympy(model.best_expr_)}")
print(f"Best mean reward     : {model.best_score_:.4f}")

[kd] Generation   1/5 | best EqGPT reward=0.9486 | expr=u_x + u_xxx + (u*u_x)_xx


[kd] Generation   2/5 | best EqGPT reward=0.9486 | expr=u_x + u_xxx + (u*u_x)_xx


[kd] Generation   3/5 | best EqGPT reward=0.9486 | expr=u_x + u_xxx + (u*u_x)_xx


[kd] Generation   4/5 | best EqGPT reward=0.9486 | expr=u_x + u_xxx + (u*u_x)_xx


[kd] Generation   5/5 | best EqGPT reward=0.9486 | expr=u_x + u_xxx + (u*u_x)_xx


[kd] Done. Best: u_x + u_xxx + (u*u_x)_xx (EqGPT reward=0.9486)


Reproduced structure : u_x + u_xxx + (u*u_x)_xx
Best mean reward     : 0.9486

docs.title: Recovered law vs the published equation
docs.text:
The published structure is eta_t = -c1*eta_x - c2*eta_xxx - c3*(eta*eta_x)_xx (all three RHS terms). The fitted coefficients below are the primary case's least-squares fit in the declared u_t = sum(c * term) domain; every experiment gets its own coefficients (next section).

The coefficient panel shows their signs and magnitudes, with numeric labels when they span several orders of magnitude.

kd.viz.plots.plot_coefficient_bar(model.result_);

docs.title: Render the report
docs.text:
model.report draws the figures this data supports and collects them into one HTML page, displayed below. The page includes notes for figure families that cannot be drawn; the same notes are available as report.warnings.

report = model.report("../out/wave_breaking")
report

Report: ../out/wave_breaking/report.html

docs.title: Composable figure functions
docs.text:
Every figure in the report can also be drawn separately. The functions in kd.viz.plots create a figure when called without ax; passing an existing Matplotlib Axes lets you combine them in a larger layout. plot_plugin uses the algorithm's own panel names and rendering method.

EqGPT's per-case reward panel has one bar per experiment, with the same discovered structure fitted separately to each case.

kd.viz.plots.plot_plugin(model.algorithm_, "per_case_reward");

A platform figure works the same way. plot_parity puts the fitted right-hand side against the measured u_t of the primary case, one point per measurement.

kd.viz.plots.plot_parity(model.result_);

docs.title: Reproduce this run
docs.text:
The run needs pretrained GPT weights, per-case surrogate checkpoints, and the measurement pickle. KD uses local assets when configured, and otherwise resolves the weights and surrogates from its Hub mirror (with permission of the authors). The measurement pickle must already be present.

Asset Location gpt_model/PDEGPT_wave_breaking.pt KD_EQGPT_ASSET_DIR, or the Hub cache model_save/wave_breaking/95_0_<case>(Non_unit)/Net_Sin_*.pkl KD_V1_WAVE_ASSETS, or the Hub cache WaveBreaking.pkl data/hf-knowledgediscover/ under the checkout root

From examples/notebooks/:

uv run --with nbconvert python -m nbconvert --to notebook --execute --inplace wave_breaking.ipynb

To use local weight and surrogate trees, set KD_EQGPT_ASSET_DIR and KD_V1_WAVE_ASSETS to their respective asset directories before running.

docs.title: Use your own data
docs.text:
This example builds a dataset from two coordinate arrays and one field array, which is the form most simulation output and most gridded measurements already have. The other examples start from a dataset shipped with KD.

The field below is generated with NumPy to give the example concrete data. Substituting your own arrays requires no other change.

docs.title: Build the dataset
docs.text:
kd.PDEDataset.from_arrays needs three things: one 1-D array per coordinate axis, one field array shaped to those axes in order, and the name of the term that goes on the left-hand side. The full contract is under Data requirements.

import numpy as np

import kd

k = 0.1
x = np.linspace(0.0, 1.0, 128)
t = np.linspace(0.0, 0.5, 101)
X, T = np.meshgrid(x, t, indexing="ij")
u = np.exp(-(np.pi**2) * k * T) * np.sin(np.pi * X) + 0.5 * np.exp(
    -4 * (np.pi**2) * k * T
) * np.sin(2 * np.pi * X)

dataset = kd.PDEDataset.from_arrays(
    coords={"x": x, "t": t},
    fields={"u": u},
    lhs="u_t",
    name="my-data",
)
kd.preview(dataset)

Dataset: my-data
Axes:
     x | n=128  | range [0.000, 1.000] | step 0.007874 (uniform)
     t | n=101  | range [0.000, 0.500] | step 0.005 (uniform)
Fields:
     u | dtype=float64 | shape=(128, 101) | min=0.000 max=1.299 mean=0.499 (NaN=0)
LHS: u_t  (field='u', axis='t')
Status: ready to fit

kd.preview reports what KD read: the axes and their spacing, the field and its range, and the left-hand side it will fit. Status: ready to fit means the dataset satisfies the contract.

kd.viz.plots.plot_field(dataset)

docs.title: Fit an algorithm
docs.text:
Fitting is a single call. seed makes the run reproducible, and generations sets the search budget.

model = kd.Model(algorithm="sga", generations=20, seed=2, verbose=False).fit(dataset)
model

Model(algorithm='sga', fitted=True, best_expr='u_t = 0.09998*u_xx', best_score=-24.38)

The displayed second derivative u_xx identifies the heat equation the field was built from. Raw term exports spell it diff2_x(u); the same IR vocabulary is used by every algorithm and is described under Equation representation.

The displayed score is SGA-PDE AIC; lower values indicate a better fit under that criterion.

docs.title: Render the report
docs.text:
model.report writes every figure that applies to this fit, plus one HTML page collecting them. The report is displayed inline below.

model.report("../out/my_data")

Report: ../out/my_data/report.html

docs.title: Measured data
docs.text: The derivatives above came from finite differences on the grid, which suits clean simulation output. For measured data, pass derivatives="autograd" to kd.Model: KD then fits a smooth surrogate to the field and differentiates that, which handles noise and points that are not evenly spaced. The two routes are compared under Derivative sources.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Getting started -- the same workflow on a bundled benchmark, with more of the result surface explained.
  • Breaking waves -- a published result reproduced on real wave-tank measurements.
  • Algorithms -- what each of the seven searches, and a worked example for each.

docs.title: Gallery
docs.text:
Each piece is one recorded run. An algorithm in KD recovers an equation from data that KD bundles or generates, the recovered equation is integrated forward from the initial data with KD's integrator, and the page compares this prediction with the observations in a figure, a movie and the full report of the run. The script that produced each piece is in examples/gallery/ of the KD repository.

SGAKdV KdV solitons The Korteweg-de Vries equation recovered from the bundled field and integrated from the initial cosine profile through the formation of the soliton train. SGAAllen-Cahn Allen-Cahn fronts A cubic reaction-diffusion equation recovered from the bundled field and integrated from the initial profile as it separates into plateaus near u = 1 and u = -1. SGAODE Lorenz attractor The three Lorenz equations recovered from two noisy trajectories, one law per state, and integrated together from the first noisy sample.

docs.title: Allen-Cahn fronts
docs.text:
The Allen-Cahn dataset that ships with KD is a reaction-diffusion field on a periodic domain. It starts from an oscillating profile of uneven amplitude; the cubic reaction term drives each point towards u = 1 or u = -1, the weaker oscillations disappear, and the domain ends up as alternating plateaus joined by interfaces whose width is set by the small diffusion coefficient. SGA-PDE recovered the equation from this field with finite-difference derivatives, using the settings of KD's recovery test for the same family of reaction-diffusion equations and the first of that test's search seeds. The recovered equation was integrated forward from the first time slice with KD's integrator over the whole record.

\[ u_t = 0.9989\,u - 0.9987\,u^{3} + 0.002997\,u_{xx} \]

Reference law: \(u_t = u - u^{3} + 0.003\,u_{xx}\)

Quantity Value Data kd.load_allen_cahn(), 256 × 201 grid, noise-free Search SGA, 150 generations, population 20, STRidge maxit 15, str_iters 15, d_tol 0.3, seed 42 Derivatives finite differences Structure every reference term and no other term (kd.judge_law, small-term threshold 0.0001) Largest coefficient error 0.13 % (threshold 5 %) NMSE of \(u_t\) 0.000119 Forward error, t from 0 to 10 0.000867 (relative L2 over the grid, x periodic) Movie 60 of 201 time steps at 12 frames per second Command python examples/gallery/allen_cahn.py 42

docs.title: Forward integration
docs.text: The observed field (left) and the discovered equation integrated from the first time slice (middle) on one diverging color scale, with u = 0, the interface level, at the neutral midpoint; the right panel is integrated minus observed on its own symmetric scale. The integrated field reaches slightly beyond the observed range, so its panel is clipped to the shared scale, and the line under the panel gives its actual range. The profile of u over time, observed (solid) and integrated from the discovered equation (dashed). The movie shows an evenly spaced subset of the recorded time steps with both ends included; the Movie row of the table gives the count, and the note at the top right of each frame repeats it. The y range is taken from the observed field and stays fixed for the whole movie.

docs.title: Report
docs.text: The full HTML report of the same run, with the search diagnostics, the term-by-term comparison and the run configuration. Open the report on its own page.

docs.title: Script
docs.text: examples/gallery/allen_cahn.py in the KD repository runs the search with the seed given on the command line, the forward integration, both figures and the report, and writes the run record that the table above is generated from. The Command row of the table gives the exact command of this run.

docs.title: KdV solitons
docs.text:
The KdV dataset that ships with KD starts from a cosine profile on a periodic domain; the nonlinear term steepens it until it breaks into a train of solitary waves that travel at different speeds. SGA-PDE recovered the Korteweg-de Vries equation from this field with finite-difference derivatives. The recovered equation was then integrated forward from the first time slice with KD's integrator over the whole record, so the figures below compare a prediction made from the initial profile alone with the observed field.

\[ u_t = -1.000\,u\,u_{x} - 0.002500\,u_{xxx} \]

Reference law: \(u_t = -u\,u_{x} - 0.0025\,u_{xxx}\)

Quantity Value Data kd.load_kdv(), 256 × 201 grid, noise-free Search SGA, 200 generations, population 20, STRidge maxit 10, str_iters 10, d_tol 1, seed 42 Derivatives finite differences Structure every reference term and no other term (kd.judge_law, small-term threshold 0.0001) Largest coefficient error 0.005 % (threshold 5 %) NMSE of \(u_t\) 2.49e-06 Forward error, t from 0 to 1 7.93e-05 (relative L2 over the grid, x periodic) Movie 60 of 201 time steps at 12 frames per second Command python examples/gallery/kdv.py

docs.title: Forward integration
docs.text: Observed profiles of u (solid) and profiles of the discovered equation integrated from the first time slice (dashed), at eight evenly spaced times with the earliest at the bottom. Each profile is raised above the previous one by the offset stated in the title, so the vertical axis carries no values. The profile of u over time, observed (solid) and integrated from the discovered equation (dashed). The movie shows an evenly spaced subset of the recorded time steps with both ends included; the Movie row of the table gives the count, and the note at the top right of each frame repeats it. The y range is taken from the observed field and stays fixed for the whole movie.

docs.title: Report
docs.text: The full HTML report of the same run, with the search diagnostics, the term-by-term comparison and the run configuration. Open the report on its own page.

docs.title: Script
docs.text: examples/gallery/kdv.py in the KD repository runs the search, the forward integration, both figures and the report, and writes the run record that the table above is generated from. The Command row of the table gives the exact command of this run.

docs.title: Lorenz attractor
docs.text:
kd.data.generate_ode_trajectories("chaotic") integrates the Lorenz system with sigma 10, rho 28 and beta 8/3. Two of its trajectories, with Gaussian noise of 1 % of each state's standard deviation added to every state, are the only input here. A neural network fitted to each noisy trajectory supplies the time derivatives, SGA-PDE fits one law per state on the resulting regression tables, and kd.forward_error_trajectories integrates the three laws together from each trajectory's first noisy sample.

\[ \begin{aligned} \dot x &= -10.02\,x + 10.02\,y \\ \dot y &= 27.76\,x - 0.9937\,x\,z - 0.9378\,y \\ \dot z &= 0.9983\,x\,y - 2.662\,z \end{aligned} \]

Reference laws: \(\dot x = -10\,x + 10\,y\), \(\dot y = 28\,x - x\,z - y\), \(\dot z = x\,y - 2.667\,z\)

Forward errors are relative L2 errors over states and times, integrated from each trajectory's first noisy sample.

Quantity Value Data 2 trajectories of generate_ode_trajectories("chaotic"), 961 samples each, t from 0 to 8, 1 % noise on each state Derivatives a neural network fitted to the samples, differentiated by autograd on each trajectory, 2 samples trimmed at each end Search SGA, one fit per state, 200 generations, population 40, depth 4, width 5, aic_ratio 0.5, seed 1 Structure every reference term and no other term in all three laws Largest coefficient error 6.2 %, the \(y\) term of \(\dot y\) (threshold 10 %) Forward error, t up to 2.5 0.0314 (trajectory 2, the one in the state panels) Forward error, t from 0 to 8 0.518 over both trajectories (reference law from the same samples: 0.500) Movie 300 frames at 24 frames per second Command python examples/gallery/lorenz.py 1

docs.title: Forward integration
docs.text: Both trajectories in state space, observed (grey) and integrated from the discovered laws (terracotta), drawn up to the time in the title; dots mark the first samples. On a chaotic attractor nearby trajectories separate exponentially, so after the window of the next figure the integrated trajectories leave the observed ones and continue on the same attractor; the reference law integrated from the same noisy samples separates in the same way, as the forward errors in the table show. The three states of trajectory 2 against time, observed (solid) and integrated from the discovered laws (dashed), up to the end of the window given in the table. The errors of each trajectory over the full interval are in the run record. The complete trajectories over the whole interval: the observed samples, with their noise, and the integrated laws trace the same two-lobed attractor.

docs.title: Reports
docs.text: One HTML report per state law, each with the search diagnostics and the run configuration: x, y, z.

docs.text: examples/gallery/lorenz.py in the KD repository builds the noisy trajectories, fits the networks and the three laws with the seed given on the command line, integrates them, draws all three figures and the reports, and writes the run record that the table above is generated from. The Command row of the table gives the exact command of this run.

docs.title: User guide
docs.text:
Choose an algorithm for the form and layout of your data, configure a fit, and inspect the returned equation and diagnostics. The guides below cover these operations and the options for continuing or comparing runs.

Task Guide Discover an equation in the browser and inspect its results KD Studio Construct a dataset from arrays or a file Data requirements Load a benchmark or published measurement Dataset catalog Select the source of derivatives Derivative sources Prepare ODE trajectories as regression tables ODE trajectories Select an algorithm and its parameters Algorithms Fix known terms and bound the unknown ones Complete a partial equation Interpret scores and refit candidate terms for comparison Score conventions Render a report or individual figures Visualization Continue a search or branch from a checkpoint Checkpoints and resuming Compare runs across seeds, algorithms or datasets Batch experiments Run or discuss a search through a language model Experimental controller

For a first installation and fit, start with Getting started. Architecture explains the platform and its contracts. Development covers component registration and extension interfaces; the API reference lists signatures and parameters.

docs.title: Checkpoint and resume with an agent
docs.text: This walkthrough shows a short search, a saved checkpoint and a second search that continues from it. The conversation is illustrative; the checkpoints and results were produced by direct calls to the current controller tools.

docs.title: Start a session
docs.text:
Install the controller and configure an endpoint, then open an interactive session with the bundled Burgers data:

kd-agent chat --dataset burgers \
    --workspace out/agent-resume

For your own file, use:

kd-agent chat --data sample.npz \
    --workspace out/agent-resume

The file command assumes the KD NPZ layout. Other layouts can supply array mappings through --load-options.

docs.title: Run a short search
docs.text:
Enter a request such as:

Use SGA with seed 0 and population 20. Run 2 generations, save a checkpoint
at each generation, and show the equation and run ID. Then wait.

The controller passes the dataset and search settings to run_discovery. KD runs the search, saves its state and returns an equation, measurements and a run ID. The checkpoint contains the search population, random state and current best candidate; it lets a later call continue this search.

Search tool arguments 
{
  "dataset_id": "burgers",
  "algorithm": "sga",
  "params": {"generations": 2, "population": 20},
  "seed": 0,
  "checkpoint_every": 1
}

docs.title: Resume from the checkpoint
docs.text:
In the same conversation, ask:

Continue that run from its latest checkpoint for 8 more generations with
the same settings. Show the updated equation and compare the two results.

The controller passes the first run's ID as resume_from_run_id. It resolves the latest eligible checkpoint and restores the saved state before searching again. The eight generations are additional work, giving ten generations in total. The second search has its own run ID and retains a link to its parent.

Resume tool arguments

<first run ID> stands for the ID returned by the preceding call.

{
  "dataset_id": "burgers",
  "algorithm": "sga",
  "params": {"generations": 8, "population": 20},
  "resume_from_run_id": "<first run ID>",
  "checkpoint_every": 1
}

The seed is inherited from the checkpoint. Reopening the same workspace in a later kd-agent chat session also makes its recorded searches available. Checkpoint details explain eligible restore points and which parameter changes are allowed.

docs.title: Demonstration results
docs.text:
These results were produced with KD 0.8.0 on 2026-09-15. Both segments used the same Burgers data, population and seed.

Initial search

$$ u_{t} = - 0.99963 u u_{x} + 0.10054 u_{x x} $$ Resumed search

\[ u_{t} = - u u_{x} + 0.10019 u_{xx} \] Segment Generations NMSE Initial 2 0.00041698 Resumed 8 1.1178e-05

The completed second run records checkpoint_final.pt from the first search as its restore source. The first two generations were preserved; the resumed call added eight more. The native NMSE measures the equation's fit to the same time-derivative target in both segments.

Download the demonstration results for full coefficients, run IDs and checkpoint provenance.

The two segments were executed through the controller's search tool. The marked boundary separates the initial search from work performed after checkpoint restoration.

docs.title: Results and records
docs.text:
The agent can submit the resumed equation with its run ID. The report links the answer to that search and records the earlier segment as its checkpoint parent. Open out/agent-resume/report.md to inspect the equations, measurements and search history; the command prints this path when it writes the report. The report is updated after each turn. Enter /exit to leave the conversation.

The language model interprets your requests and chooses tool calls. KD carries out the numerical searches and checkpoint restoration. The saved records make it possible to inspect which checkpoint was used and how much additional work was performed. If the model edits an equation before submitting it, the report keeps that submission separate from the recorded equation and its measurements.

The controller guide covers endpoint settings and run budgets. The architecture page describes how the controller uses KD's public interfaces.

docs.title: Agent guide
docs.text:
The experimental kd-agent controller uses a language model to select and run KD algorithms, inspect their results and continue searches from checkpoints. It accepts a catalog dataset or a data file and writes a Markdown report in the run workspace.

The agent example shows a short search and continuation from a saved checkpoint, with results from both segments. The sections below cover installation, input formats and run options.

docs.title: Install and configure
docs.text:
In the activated environment from Installation, install the controller with uv:

uv pip install "sail-kd[agent]" --torch-backend=auto

Or use pip:

python -m pip install "sail-kd[agent]"

With pip on a machine with a GPU, install the PyTorch build for the driver first, as described under CUDA PyTorch.

Then configure the language-model endpoint:

kd-agent setup

Setup asks for an endpoint, base URL, model and API key. OpenAI-compatible and Anthropic endpoints are supported. The settings are saved in ~/.config/kd/agent.json and reused by run and chat. Run setup again to change the saved settings. PySR searches also require sail-kd[pysr]; install sail-kd[agent,pysr] when using both components.

docs.title: Run a search
docs.text:
Pass a data file and a request:

kd-agent run --data sample.npz \
    "Find the equation governing this data."

Here, sample.npz uses the KD NPZ layout. To try a bundled benchmark, use its catalog identifier:

kd-agent run --dataset burgers --workspace out/agent-burgers \
    "Find the equation governing this data."

The file is loaded through kd.load. A registered layout supplies the mapping; other files require the coordinate, field and left-hand-side choices described in data requirements. Pass these choices as JSON:

kd-agent run --data run.mat \
    --load-options '{"coords":{"x":"x","t":"t"},"fields":{"u":"usol"},"lhs":"u_t"}'

For a PDEBench file with several samples, select one explicitly:

kd-agent run --data 1D_Burgers_Sols_Nu0.01.hdf5 \
    --load-options '{"select":{"sample":0}}'

docs.title: Discuss a search
docs.text:
kd-agent chat --data sample.npz --workspace out/agent-chat

The interactive session accepts follow-up requests about the results and search choices. Supplying an existing --workspace reuses its run ledger and recorded searches. For example, ask:

Inspect the data and find an equation for u_t.

After a result, a follow-up can request another search:

Try another suitable algorithm and compare the equations it finds.

docs.title: Results and run options
docs.text:
The command prints its workspace path. A one-shot run also prints report_path and stop_reason; open the report to read the selected equation, search history and stopping outcome. Without --workspace, the command creates a directory under kd-agent-runs/ in the current directory.

--endpoint, --base-url and --model override the saved choices for a run. --time-budget-minutes communicates a budget to the model and supplies the remaining budget to searches; it is not a timeout for the whole conversation. --recursion-limit bounds the controller's execution steps. Use kd-agent run --help or kd-agent chat --help for the command options. Help works with the base installation; running the controller requires the extra.

docs.title: Complete a partial equation
docs.text: A sketch states what is already known about an equation before the search starts: terms whose coefficients are fixed, terms that must appear with coefficients fitted from the data, and room for a bounded number of unknown terms. Model.fit(sketch=...) passes it to the algorithm, and the result reports whether the selected law satisfies every clause.

docs.title: Write a sketch
docs.text:
kd.Sketch takes three keyword clauses, any of which may be omitted, but not all of them:

import kd

data = kd.load_burgers()
sketch = kd.Sketch(
    pinned={"u*u_x": -1.0},
    holes=[kd.Hole(max_terms=1, max_deriv_order=2)],
)
model = kd.Model(algorithm="sga", generations=50, seed=0).fit(data, sketch=sketch)
outcome = model.result_.sketch_outcome
  • pinned maps a term to its fixed coefficient. The pinned terms are subtracted from the regression target before the search and restored with their exact coefficients afterwards. A pinned coefficient must be finite and nonzero.
  • anchored lists terms that must appear in the law; their coefficients are fitted from the data, for example anchored=["u_xx"].
  • holes lists kd.Hole objects. A hole admits between min_terms (default 1) and max_terms terms beyond the pinned and anchored ones, each with a total derivative order of at most max_deriv_order, built only from the operators in operators and only from the fields in fields. A constraint left at None is not checked. Operators are named as in the law representation ("mul", "recip", "n2", "n3"; division is {"mul", "recip"}), and an empty collection admits only terms without operators. Several holes in one sketch need disjoint fields.

With pinned terms, model.best_expr_ holds the expression the algorithm searched, without them; model.result_.equation and the outcome's laws include them.

docs.title: Term notation
docs.text: A term string is a name (u, u_xx), a product (u*u_x), a positive integer power (u**2, the product u*u), or KD's function-call notation (mul(u,u_x), diff2_x(u), n2(u)), and these forms can be mixed. n2 and n3 are separate operators that clip their input, so n2(u) and u**2 are different terms. Spellings of the same term, such as u_x*u and mul(u_x,u), are one term. A fixed coefficient is the value of a pinned entry and the constant column is the name one; sums, infix division, unary minus and ^ are refused, and add(...), div(...) and neg(...) remain available in function-call notation. The notation is described under Equation representation.

docs.title: Resolution against a dataset
docs.text: kd.Sketch called with these keywords returns a kd.SketchSpec, which holds the term strings, the pinned coefficients and the holes without reference to a dataset. Model.fit and kd.harness.run_episode resolve it against the dataset they fit: the left-hand side, the vocabulary (every field and axis of the dataset) and an exact match policy are taken from the dataset unless they are given. spec.resolve(dataset) performs the same step and returns the complete sketch, which is part of the run's identity for checkpoints and resuming. Each term is checked against the dataset's fields and axes when the sketch is resolved; a term that cannot be evaluated raises and names its clause, for example anchored[0] or pinned['u*u_x']. Resolution computes nothing on the data, so one spec can be resolved against several datasets.

docs.title: Algorithm support
docs.text:
A sketch applies to evolution data and to tables. On a kd.TabularDataset, including an ODE system converted with kd.data.trajectories_to_tabular, the left-hand side is the target column, the vocabulary is the feature columns, and the intercept is the term one. A hole on a table cannot bound the derivative order, and a feature name that contains an underscore is refused. A law fitted on a table is compared with the sketch term by term: products and the powers n2 and n3 of sums are multiplied out, the result is split at its additions, and numeric factors become part of each coefficient, so x1*(x2 + 0.5) is the two terms x1*x2 and x1.

On a table, a product counts as one term regardless of how its factors are grouped, so mul(x1,mul(x2,x3)) and mul(mul(x1,x2),x3) are the same term. n2 and n3 of a sum are counted by their monomials only when the law is compared with the sketch; the certified law keeps the fitted n2 or n3 term, so its input is still clipped.

Each mode of each algorithm declares, clause by clause, how far it enforces a sketch, in the sketch block of its entry in kd.instrument_schemas(). Platform and plugins shows that block and the meaning of its levels. A sketch that uses a clause the selected mode does not support raises at fit(), before the search starts.

docs.title: Read the outcome
docs.text:
model.result_.sketch_outcome holds four parts:

  • solution, the certified law. It is set only when the selected law satisfies every clause and fits the data within the verify policy of the fit; by default that policy is kd.SKETCH_EXIT_VERIFY, which requires an NMSE of at most 0.05.
  • best_candidate, the best law found, whether or not it was certified.
  • verdict, the clause-by-clause match of the selected law.
  • failure, the reason when no solution was certified.

A certified solution means that the clauses and the residual condition hold for that law on the fitted dataset. fit(..., verify=kd.VerifyPolicy()) removes the residual threshold; a verification that cannot be computed still withholds the solution.

docs.title: Save and load a sketch
docs.text:
Save the specification above as a JSON file, then load it for another fit:

kd.save_sketch(sketch, "burgers-sketch.json")
loaded = kd.load_sketch("burgers-sketch.json")
model.fit(data, sketch=loaded)

An unbound specification keeps its term strings and constraints; fit resolves them against the dataset. To bind the file immediately, pass dataset=data to kd.load_sketch. A complete sketch also records its left-hand side and vocabulary, which must match the dataset used later.

docs.title: Use a sketch with kd-agent
docs.text:
After installing and configuring the controller, pass the same file through --sketch:

kd-agent run --data burgers --sketch burgers-sketch.json "Find the missing diffusion term."

The controller binds the sketch to the loaded data. Its selected search mode must support the requested clauses, just as with Model.fit. This command uses the configured language-model endpoint.

docs.title: Worked example
docs.text: The Burgers sketch script pins the advection coefficient, searches for the remaining terms, and reads the clause-by-clause outcome. On gridded evolution data, DISCOVER's PINN mode also accepts sketches: pinned terms enter its residual with fixed coefficients and anchored terms with fitted coefficients. EqGPT's multi-case wave and steady modes refuse sketches. On tables, PySINDy and LLM4ED accept the supported tabular clauses; consult the mode's schema before selecting other combinations.

docs.title: KD Studio
docs.text:
KD Studio provides data loading, search configuration, result inspection and comparison in a local browser workspace. This guide uses a recorded SGA-PDE search on Burgers data in KD 0.10.0, followed by verification and comparison with another algorithm. It also covers saved runs and workspace history.

The KD Studio quick start covers installation and a first search. The project README links the video of the recorded search.

Preview Installation

Burgers field in KD Studio preview. The preview includes data, preprocessing and algorithm settings.

docs.title: Start a workspace
docs.text:
KD Studio supports Linux, WSL and Windows. In an activated Python 3.11+ environment, install the UI extra and start KD:

uv pip install "sail-kd[ui]" --torch-backend=auto
kd-ui --workspace ./kd-ui-workspace

With pip, use python -m pip install "sail-kd[ui]". The installation guide covers environment creation, activation and PyTorch builds. Open the full URL printed in the terminal; it signs your browser into this workspace. Keep the terminal open while using the interface. KD serves the pages on your own machine.

docs.title: Choose and inspect data
docs.text:
On Data, select burgers in the catalog. The field preview shows u on a grid of 256 spatial points and 201 time points. Keep the default field view for this walkthrough. The axes and field statistics help you check that KD has read the intended values and coordinates.

The reference equation is hidden until you choose Show reference equation. Leave it hidden during this walkthrough; the search takes the observed field as input. For your own measurements, choose File, upload a file or enter its local path, inspect the arrays, and map coordinates, fields and the left-hand side. Data requirements explains the supported layouts and file mappings.

The separate Time slices view is available for inspecting individual profiles.

docs.title: Prepare the search input
docs.text:
Choose Continue to Prepare. This page exposes derivative and smoothing choices, along with previews of their effects. For the bundled clean Burgers example, keep finite differences and no smoothing. Continue to Search.

For noisy measurements, inspect the original and prepared fields before launching a search. A smoothing choice belongs to that run's configuration; the original dataset remains available for comparison.

docs.title: Configure and launch SGA
docs.text:
The Prepare page preselects compatible algorithm modes. In the algorithm list, uncheck the other selected modes and keep only sga default. Set generations to 20 and Seeds to 0, leaving the other algorithm parameters at their defaults. The parameters are taken from KD's algorithm schemas. Review the memory and time limits; the recording uses a 4 GiB cap and a two-minute soft time budget. Choose Check settings and Queue 1 run.

The Queued panel appears after submission. Click the job link in its first column to open the live run page. The header navigation also keeps the data, preparation and search pages available.

Each selected algorithm, mode and seed produces its own job. You can submit several seeds together; the queue runs fits one at a time by default. The run page reports the phase, the best expression so far and the algorithm's score history. The progress curve below belongs to the recorded 20-generation run.

docs.title: Inspect the equation and checks
docs.text:
When the run is complete, click Open result at the top of the run page. The page shows the selected equation and its coefficients, the algorithm's native score and the fit metrics. Fit leads to figures such as the coefficient chart, expression tree, residuals and field comparisons; Report opens the generated HTML report. Report compatibility records the environment used for this walkthrough and the report-export workaround.

Read the verification checks separately:

  • Term ablation removes one term at a time and measures the resulting fit error. It indicates how much the fitted law depends on each term.
  • Block dispersion compares coefficients fitted on separate spatial blocks. It describes variation across those blocks.
  • Forward simulation integrates the equation and compares its predicted field with the observations. Request this check from the verification panel; it runs as a separate queued operation.

A small residual alone does not establish that the equation reproduces the field over time. The report explanation explains the distinction between the residual and forward prediction.

docs.title: Compare with another algorithm
docs.text:
Return to Search, select only pysindy default, keep seed 0 and the default parameters, and queue the run on the same dataset without smoothing. From the result pages, choose Add to comparison, or select both completed runs on Compare. Choose Re-measure in the shared frame.

Use the shared-frame NMSE to compare the fitted equations on the same data. The table also preserves each algorithm's native score under its own name; SGA's AIC and PySINDy's native score are not the same quantity. The score guide explains the remeasurement.

To try another setting, use Edit and rerun. KD opens the previous configuration for editing and keeps the new run separate from its source.

docs.title: Return to the workspace
docs.text:
Uploads, datasets and run history are stored in kd-ui-workspace. Stop the web server with Ctrl+C. Next time, run the same command with the same workspace path and open the newly printed URL. All runs and history lists the saved runs; the comparison and result pages can be reopened without repeating a fit.

You can also add a directory containing runs made outside the UI through the run-folder controls. For scripted experiments, continue with the Quick start; for language-model-assisted discovery, see the controller guide.

docs.title: Get started with KD
docs.text: This example installs KD and fits an equation to the bundled Burgers field. The KD Studio quick start covers the browser interface; the experimental agent guide covers language-model-assisted searches.

docs.title: Install KD
docs.text:
KD requires Python 3.11 or later. Create an environment:

python -m venv .venv
Linux / macOS / WSLWindows (PowerShell) 
source .venv/bin/activate

.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1

Install KD in that environment:

python -m pip install "sail-kd==0.10.0" "matplotlib==3.10.8"

The Matplotlib pin keeps HTML reports working with KD 0.10.0. The installation reference covers uv, CPU/CUDA builds and extras.

docs.title: Fit a bundled dataset
docs.text:
Run this in a Python script or notebook:

import kd
# Bundled Burgers field: 256 × 201 (x, t)
data = kd.load_burgers()

model = kd.Model(
    algorithm="sga", generations=5, seed=0
).fit(data)
Recorded result · 5 generations · AIC -28.78 \(u_t =\)\(-u\,u_x\)\(+0.1002\,u_{xx}\)

The equation above is the recorded result of this five-generation example. model.result_.equation gives the fitted equation in Python.

docs.title: Read the report
docs.text:
report = model.report("out/first-fit")

Open out/first-fit/report.html in a browser. In a notebook, display report as the last expression of a cell. The Quick start explains the equation, native score, residual and forward prediction separately.

docs.title: KD Studio
docs.text: The KD Studio quick start covers installation, data loading and a first search. The preview provides sample data and editable settings in the browser without installation.

docs.title: Use your own data
docs.text: Data requirements explains how to construct datasets from arrays or inspect and map the contents of a file. The own-data notebook shows the array workflow.

docs.title: Further documentation
docs.text:
• Quick start: the full first-fit tutorial and report interpretation.
  • KD Studio quick start: the first search through the local browser interface.
  • User guide: preprocessing, parameters, partial equations and experiments.
  • Tutorials: longer searches and experimental data.
  • Documentation: guides and API reference.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
KD requires Python 3.11 or later. The distribution is named sail-kd; Python code imports it as kd.

For a first search, follow the Quick start or KD Studio quick start. This page is the installation reference for environment setup, PyTorch builds and extras.

Interface Package selection Python scripts and notebooks sail-kd KD Studio sail-kd[ui] Experimental agent controller sail-kd[agent]

docs.title: Install KD
docs.text:
The shortest installation on Linux and macOS creates a virtual environment, activates it and installs KD with pip:

python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install sail-kd

In Windows PowerShell, the activation command is:

.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1

Activate the environment in each new shell before running the Python examples or kd-agent.

uv can be used instead of pip. uv venv creates .venv, and with --torch-backend=auto uv selects the PyTorch build for the available hardware: a CUDA build the installed driver supports, or the CPU build. Activate .venv afterwards with the command for your platform.

pipuv 
python -m pip install sail-kd

uv venv
uv pip install sail-kd --torch-backend=auto

docs.title: CPU PyTorch
docs.text:
For a Linux environment that will use CPU PyTorch, install that build before KD:

python -m pip install torch --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cpu

Then install KD with the pip command above. With uv, replace --torch-backend=auto with --torch-backend=cpu.

docs.title: CUDA PyTorch
docs.text:
A CUDA build of PyTorch runs only with a driver that supports its CUDA version. pip install sail-kd resolves the newest CUDA build on PyPI; on a machine whose driver is older, torch.cuda.is_available() returns False and KD runs on the CPU. Install the build for the driver first, from the PyTorch index for that CUDA version, then install KD with the pip command above:

python -m pip install torch --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu128

With uv, --torch-backend=auto reads the driver and selects a supported build; a specific build can be named instead, for example --torch-backend=cu128.

docs.title: KD Studio
docs.text:
The local browser interface supports Linux (including WSL) and Windows. In your activated environment, install the ui extra and start a workspace:

uv pip install "sail-kd[ui]" --torch-backend=auto
kd-ui --workspace ./kd-ui-workspace

With pip, use python -m pip install "sail-kd[ui]". Open the URL printed in the terminal to load data, configure searches, inspect results and compare runs. The workspace stores uploads, datasets and run history. Stop the server with Ctrl+C; start it with the same workspace to reopen those records.

The KD Studio walkthrough follows a real Burgers search, from choosing the data to comparing the resulting equations. It includes interface screenshots, a preview link and the settings used in the example.

Report compatibility

The KD Studio walkthrough was recorded with KD 0.10.0 and Matplotlib 3.10.8. With KD 0.10.0, Matplotlib 3.11.2 causes HTML report generation to fail after a successful fit. Use Matplotlib 3.10.8 for report export if you encounter this error. The issue is separate from equation discovery.

docs.title: PySR and the controller
docs.text:
PySR requires an extra and downloads a Julia runtime on first use:

python -m pip install "sail-kd[pysr]"

The experimental language-model controller requires the agent extra:

python -m pip install "sail-kd[agent]"

For PySR searches through the controller, install sail-kd[agent,pysr]. With uv, the same extras install with uv pip install "sail-kd[agent]" --torch-backend=auto.

docs.title: Language-model endpoints and downloaded assets
docs.text:
Three components use resources outside the installed package, and each is configured on its own:

  • The controller calls the language-model endpoint saved by kd-agent setup. The controller guide describes endpoint configuration, data selection and run reports.
  • LLM4ED calls an OpenAI-compatible endpoint during its search. In Python it uses the base_url of its Llm4edConfig and the API key in the OPENAI_API_KEY environment variable, or a provider object passed to the algorithm; it does not read the controller's saved settings. The LLM4ED page describes the setup.
  • EqGPT downloads its pretrained model assets on first use, as described on the EqGPT page.

docs.title: Check the installation
docs.text:
python -c "import kd; print(kd.__version__)"
kd-agent --help

The command's help is available with the base installation. Controller runs require the extra above.

Continue with the first fit, or read data requirements before loading your own observations.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
This tutorial installs KD, fits an equation to the bundled Burgers dataset and explains the resulting report. The first-fit notebook uses the same configuration.

For the browser interface, see KD Studio quick start and the KD Studio guide, which covers verification and comparison. The experimental agent guide covers language-model-assisted searches.

docs.title: Install KD
docs.text:
On Linux and macOS, create and activate a virtual environment and install the sail-kd distribution:

python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install "sail-kd==0.10.0" "matplotlib==3.10.8"

The Matplotlib pin keeps HTML reports working with KD 0.10.0. Installation gives the Windows activation command, the uv route, the CPU and CUDA builds of PyTorch and the optional components.

docs.title: Fit a bundled dataset
docs.text:
import kd
# Bundled Burgers field: 256 × 201 (x, t)
data = kd.load_burgers()

model = kd.Model(
    algorithm="sga", generations=5, seed=0
).fit(data)
Recorded result · 5 generations · AIC -28.78 \(u_t =\)\(-u\,u_x\)\(+0.1002\,u_{xx}\)

kd.load_burgers() returns the Burgers benchmark as a PDEDataset: the field u on a grid of 256 points in x and 201 in t. kd.Model selects SGA-PDE and runs five generations of its search with a fixed seed, printing the best equation after each generation. With this recipe the fit returns u_t = -u*u_x + 0.1002*u_xx, which print(model.result_.equation) shows; the dataset's reference equation is u_t = -u*u_x + 0.1*u_xx.

docs.title: Read the report
docs.text:
report = model.report("out/first-fit")

model.report writes every figure the fit supports and one HTML page into out/first-fit/. Open out/first-fit/report.html in a browser, or leave report as the last expression of a notebook cell to display the page inline. The report separates four quantities that answer different questions:

  • The equation is the law the search selected, with its terms and fitted coefficients. The equation card and the coefficient bar chart show the coefficients; the card compares them with the reference equation when the dataset carries one.
  • The native score is the number the algorithm optimizes, here the AIC of SGA-PDE, where lower is better. It ranks candidates within one search and is not comparable across algorithms.
  • The residual compares the time derivative estimated from the data with the right-hand side of the equation evaluated at the same points. The parity plot, the residual figure and the PDE residual field show it; the NMSE in the metadata table at the top of the report summarizes it.
  • The forward prediction integrates the discovered equation in time from the first observed time slice and compares the resulting field with the measured one. The field comparison, the time slices and the error heatmap show it. Errors in the right-hand side accumulate during integration, so this comparison tests the equation as a model of the field rather than of its derivative.

The remaining figures describe the search itself. The warnings section lists the figures that were skipped or degraded, together with other notes from rendering, such as the boundary condition used for integration. Figure generation describes each figure, and Score conventions describes how candidate terms are refitted against the same data before equations from different runs or algorithms are compared.

docs.title: Use your own data
docs.text: For a file of your own, data requirements describes kd.inspect_file, the registered file layouts and the array mappings kd.load accepts.

docs.title: Core examples
docs.text: notebook First fit Load the data, fit an algorithm, and read the result. notebook Use your own data Two coordinate arrays and one field array, from NumPy to a fitted equation. notebook Noisy data The Burgers benchmark with 15% Gaussian noise added, with derivatives taken from a network fitted to the noisy field. kd.Sketch(pinned={"u*u_x": -1.0},holes=[kd.Hole(max_terms=1)]) guide Complete a partial equation Fix the known terms, require others, and bound the number of unknown terms. kd-agent run \--data sample.npz \"Find the governing equation." command lineexperimental Agent search Run a short search, save a checkpoint and continue from it, with the results of both segments.

docs.title: Experimental controller
docs.text: The controller guide covers a first run with kd-agent: install the extra, configure an endpoint, select a dataset and read the report. The controller can also discuss a search interactively.

docs.title: Further documentation
docs.text:
Use the user guide for algorithm configuration, score interpretation, figures, checkpoints and batch experiments. The tutorials include KdV, noisy Burgers, breaking waves and chromatography.

The architecture page contains the complete component diagram, import layers and execution order of a fit. Design introduces the platform and plugin responsibilities behind that diagram.

docs.title: KD Studio quick start
docs.text:
This guide installs KD Studio and runs an SGA-PDE search on the bundled Burgers dataset. KD Studio runs locally in a browser and supports Linux, WSL and Windows. It requires Python 3.11 or later.

For scripts and notebooks, see Quick start. The experimental agent guide covers language-model-assisted searches.

Preview Studio guide

Burgers field in KD Studio preview. Searches run in the installed application.

docs.title: Install KD
docs.text:
With uv installed, create an environment:

uv venv --python 3.11

Activate it in the same terminal:

Linux / WSLWindows (PowerShell) 
source .venv/bin/activate

.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1

Install KD Studio:

uv pip install "sail-kd[ui]" --torch-backend=auto

The installation reference covers pip, CPU/CUDA builds and optional components.

docs.title: Start KD Studio
docs.text:
kd-ui --workspace ./kd-ui-workspace

Open the full URL printed in the terminal, including its #token part. Keep this terminal open while using the interface. The workspace directory stores your datasets and runs; start with the same path to reopen them later.

docs.title: Fit a bundled dataset
docs.text:
1. On Data, select burgers. Check the field preview, then click Continue to Prepare.
  2. Keep finite differences and no smoothing. Click Continue to Search.
  3. Keep only sga default selected. Set generations to 20 and Seeds to 0. Leave the remaining parameters at their defaults.
  4. Click Check settings, then Queue 1 run. Open the job link in the Queued panel to watch its progress.

The run page shows the best equation so far and the search's score history. When the run completes, click Open result.

docs.title: Read the report
docs.text:
The recorded burgers example used SGA-PDE, 20 generations and seed 0:

\[ u_{t} = - u u_{x} + 0.1002 u_{xx} \]

The result page shows the fitted equation, coefficients and checks. Use Fit to inspect the figures and Report to open or download the HTML report. The Forward simulation check tests the equation's time evolution separately from its fit to derivatives. Report compatibility covers the recorded environment and the known report-export issue.

The KD Studio guide explains these panels, verification, comparisons and run history. The report explanation distinguishes the native score, residual and forward prediction.

docs.title: Use your own data
docs.text: Choose File on the Data page, inspect the arrays or columns, and map the coordinates, fields and target. Data requirements describes supported layouts and formats. The bundled Burgers dataset can be used to check the setup before loading your own measurements.

docs.title: Other interfaces
docs.text: Interface Start here Python scripts and notebooks Quick start Experimental language-model controller Agent guide

docs.title: Further documentation
docs.text: Use the user guide for preprocessing, algorithm settings, partial equations, figures, checkpoints and batch experiments. The tutorials cover longer searches and experimental data; Documentation lists the guides and reference pages.

docs.title: Visualization
docs.text: KD provides a common visualization interface across algorithms. Each algorithm can also expose diagnostic figures for its own search process, including population statistics, policy training, language-model proposals and sparse fits. This page explains the shared figure types and the algorithm-specific diagnostics. Figure generation covers the calls for your own run; the figure gallery contains all figures and reading notes from one SGA-PDE run.

docs.title: Platform figures
docs.text:
Whichever algorithm ran, VizEngine draws the same group: best score per iteration, measured against predicted, the equation typeset and as a structure tree, the fitted coefficients, and the residual as a histogram and as a spatial map. Pass the dataset as well and it adds the field comparison, the u_t residual field, time slices and an error heatmap.

The six figures below come from one run: SGA-PDE on the KdV dataset that ships with KD, 200 generations, seed 42.

The observed field over its physical spatial and time coordinates. The fitted derivative target, its equation prediction, and predicted minus measured values. The first two panels share a color scale; the residual has its own scale, with any clipping disclosed on the figure. Predicted values against the measured target, with the diagonal denoting exact agreement and R² computed over the full fit. The best native score is shown above the algorithm's population diagnostic, when one is recorded. Each panel retains its own score scale. The active fitted coefficients, retaining their signs and any scale changes disclosed by the axis. The active equation's operators and derivatives, with coefficient magnitudes shown separately.

model.report("out/report") renders the supported figures into one HTML file, with captions, settings and raw result JSON. In a notebook, the returned report is displayed inline. Browse the figure gallery or open the SGA-PDE report. Every algorithm page links its own report.

docs.title: Algorithm panels
docs.text:
The shared figures describe the fitted equation and its residuals. Each algorithm also declares diagnostic panels for its search or fitting procedure:

  • SGA-PDE, DLGA-PDE: population-level records, per generation the diversity of the candidates, the term count of the candidate equations and the score spread of the survivors, plus the training loss of the neural-network surrogate (filled in only when the platform trained one). SGA-PDE also draws the genome tree of its best individual.
  • DISCOVER: the policy network's training record, per iteration the reward (one curve for the elite subset, one for the full batch), the entropy regularizer and the reward baseline.
  • EqGPT: the reward of the candidate pool per epoch and its spread, plus the cross-entropy loss of each epoch's fine-tune. In multi-case mode it adds the reward of the discovered structure on every case.
  • LLM4ED: the reward spread of the candidate pool per round, the count of invalid candidates, and the cumulative number of language-model calls.
  • PySR: the Pareto front (complexity against loss), KD's independent re-score of that same front, and the two scores against each other.
  • PySINDy: one comparison figure putting the NMSE of PySINDy's native coefficients next to the NMSE of KD's independent refit.

Each row below is one algorithm's panels, from that algorithm's own worked run.

The algorithm's diagnostic panels, using the same data and plot functions as the full report. The algorithm's diagnostic panels, using the same data and plot functions as the full report. The algorithm's diagnostic panels, using the same data and plot functions as the full report. The algorithm's diagnostic panels, using the same data and plot functions as the full report. The algorithm's diagnostic panels, using the same data and plot functions as the full report.

docs.title: Data shape
docs.text:
Which figures a run gets follows from the shape of its data rather than from the algorithm. Data on a regular grid gets the whole set. Scattered measurements carry point coordinates and no grid, so the field family is left out and the rest draws as usual; the breaking-waves example is a run of that kind. A table of X against y has no field at all, and the coefficient bar follows whether the run returned an equation rather than on the shape of the data. Two-dimensional space plus time adds one more: pass animate=True and render_all writes a GIF of the field evolving.

Whatever is left out is named in report.warnings, one note per figure family, and the same notes appear on the report page.

docs.title: Figure index
docs.text:
Every figure KD draws, and the call that draws just that one. The platform half runs for any result; the rest belong to the algorithm named beside them. Two are composed at render time and are not listed: SGA-PDE's genome tree, and EqGPT's panels in multi-case and steady mode. At run time plugin.list_plots() returns the complete set for the algorithm that ran.

docs.title: Figure gallery
docs.text:
These figures come from the SGA-PDE worked example. Each image and its reading note is taken directly from that run's full HTML report. Field predictions come from forward integration; derivative predictions are evaluated on the search target.

In a notebook, model.report("out/report") displays the complete report inline. The same returned object lists the saved figures and any rendering notes.

Convergence. Read the best native score reached at each search iteration. Parity. Compare predicted and observed targets against the diagonal of exact agreement. Equation. Read the published equation with its fitted coefficients and active terms. Equation Tree. Read the operators and derivatives that compose the published equation. Residual. Read the distribution and spatial pattern of predicted minus observed target values. Coefficient Bar. Compare the magnitudes and signs of the active fitted coefficients. Field Comparison. Compare the measured field with forward integration of the discovered equation and their difference. Pde Residual Field. Compare the fitted derivative target with the equation prediction and their residual, without forward integration. Time Slices. Compare measured and integrated fields at the labeled observation times. Error Heatmap. Locate the signed field error from forward integration at the labeled physical coordinates. Offspring Diversity. Distinct candidate-expression count among this generation's evaluated offspring (the staged batch, post-dedup; failed evaluations count too). A collapsing count signals premature convergence / loss of search diversity. NOT a population statistic — the count can exceed the population size. Complexity Evolution. Mean number of STRidge-selected (non-zero) terms across this generation's valid offspring — a sparsity / bloat monitor for the evolving PDE candidates. All-invalid generations appear as gaps (nothing was measured). Fitness Spread. Per-generation MEAN AIC over the surviving population's finite scores (lower is better). The platform 'convergence' plot draws the single best AIC; this curve shows the level of the whole surviving population — under elitist truncation it declines alongside the best curve, and the distance between the two is how far the population trails its optimum. Generations with no finite-scored survivors (e.g. an all-invalid start) appear as gaps (their +inf sentinel is masked). Surrogate Training Curve. FieldModel surrogate training loss vs epoch (log-y): train and — when a validation split exists — validation MSE, with the best-validation epoch marked. The autograd derivatives (u_x, u_t) the GA reads from come from this network. Absent (No data panel) for finite-diff mode or when the surrogate was pre-trained (user-supplied field_model), not trained by the platform builder. Genome Tree. Raw GP genome of the best individual — operator names (*, ^2, d) as the genetic operators produced them, pre-canonicalization. Shows all evolved terms before STRidge pruning, so its term count may exceed the discovered equation's (Expression Tree). Unavailable for results loaded from disk (no live population).

docs.title: Figure generation
docs.text: After fit, model.report renders the supported figures and a report. Individual plotting calls place a panel on an Axes supplied by the caller. Both use the data recorded during the fit, without additional recorder setup.

docs.title: One call
docs.text:
import kd

dataset = kd.load_kdv()
model = kd.Model(algorithm="sga", generations=200, seed=42).fit(dataset)

report = model.report("out/kdv")

print(report.report)
for path in report.figures:
    print(path.name)

In a notebook, leave report as the last expression in the cell to display its HTML page inline. print(model.result_.equation) uses mathematical notation; model.best_expr_, the equation's terms, and JSON exports retain the raw IR. The gallery shows the figures and captions from one complete run.

Output (out/kdv is created if it does not exist):

out/kdv/report.html
convergence.svg
parity.svg
equation.svg
equation_tree.svg
residual.svg
coefficient_bar.svg
field_comparison.svg
pde_residual_field.svg
time_slices.svg
error_heatmap.svg
plugin_population_diversity.svg
plugin_complexity_evolution.svg
plugin_fitness_spread.svg
plugin_surrogate_training.svg
plugin_genome_tree.svg

The lower-level VizEngine.render_all call takes the result, algorithm and dataset explicitly. It reads the result's per-iteration records and the algorithm's declared diagnostic panels:

kd.VizEngine(output_dir="out/kdv").render_all(
    model.result_, algorithm=model.algorithm_, dataset=dataset
)

Three arguments to render_all control the output:

  • algorithm= takes the fitted algorithm itself, which draws its own diagnostic panels; those filenames carry the plugin_ prefix. Leave it out and only the universal figures are rendered.
  • dataset= decides whether the data-dependent figures are drawn: the coefficient bar chart, the field comparison, the u_t residual field, the time slices and the error heatmap.
  • animate=True additionally writes a GIF for 2D-spatial-plus-time data, with its path in report.data_files.

Skips and degradations go into report.warnings, so the figure set never shrinks silently. The run above produced exactly one:

plugin plot 'surrogate_training': No data (no surrogate training logged for this run)

That line comes from the algorithm's own plotting code: this run took derivatives by finite difference, trained no surrogate network, and the panel is therefore empty.

report.report points at an HTML report with every figure inlined as SVG, so it travels as a single file. Its equations are drawn as inline SVG, so they read without a network; when the browser is online, MathJax from a public CDN typesets them. The report this page's run writes is published here: example report, 15 figures in 1.7 MB. The style= argument of VizEngine takes extra matplotlib rcParams and merges them over KD's defaults. To put several runs side by side, call viz.render_comparison(results, labels=[...]): the convergence curves are overlaid, plus a bar chart of R² across the runs and a summary table.

docs.title: A single panel
docs.text:
To place one panel in a layout of your own, create the Axes and hand it to the algorithm:

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

plugin = model.algorithm_
print([info.name for info in plugin.list_plots()])

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 3))
plugin.render_plot("complexity_evolution", ax)
fig.savefig("complexity.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches="tight")

data = plugin.get_plot_data("complexity_evolution")
print(data["ylabel"], data["y"][:5])

Output:

['population_diversity', 'complexity_evolution', 'fitness_spread', 'surrogate_training', 'genome_tree']
gen_mean_complexity [1.8235294117647058, 2.34375, 3.242424242424242, 3.026315789473684, 3.6]

The Figure belongs to the caller: render_plot draws only on the Axes it is given, so size, colors and titles remain under the caller's control. It returns the degradation notes for that panel (no data, gaps in the series), and merging those into report.warnings is what render_all does with them.

get_plot_data returns the numbers behind the same panel, ready to serialize to JSON and hand to another plotting library or keep as a record. Its fields depend on the panel; a per-generation curve is {x, y, xlabel, ylabel, title}.

An unknown name raises, listing the names this algorithm has:

Unknown plot name: 'nope'. Available: population_diversity, complexity_evolution, fitness_spread, surrogate_training, genome_tree

For another algorithm, change algorithm= and re-run: list_plots() then returns that algorithm's panels, and both paths above are written the same way.
